name: Hepatocellular adenoma
lead: Which gate this patient is at — whether the lesion is really an adenoma and of which subtype, whether sex or size or growth has earned an operation yet, and how long risk-factor modification is allowed to run before you call it a failure. Read the size gate knowing what the full-text read established: 5 cm is a convention, not a derived threshold, and six months is too early to call the trial a failure.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 1 · Is this an adenoma, and which one
crit: Contrast-enhanced MRI, preferably with a hepatobiliary agent, including fat-sensitive and chemical-shift sequences
Every measurable lesion counted, with dominant diameter, exophytic protrusion, segment and vascular relationships recorded
Risk-factor history taken explicitly: oestrogen, anabolic androgens, BMI, alcohol, glycogen storage disease, vascular liver disease, family history
Subtype assigned where imaging allows it, and recorded as unassigned where it does not
An at-risk liver excluded — cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B or prior HCC puts this on the HCC pathway, not this one
gates.ask: Am I sure this is an adenoma rather than focal nodular hyperplasia or a well-differentiated carcinoma, and do I know which subtype I am dealing with?

standard.t: Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI, and use a hepatobiliary contrast agent where the question is adenoma versus focal nodular hyperplasia.
standard.pref: Every patient at presentation. EASL 2016 states that MRI is superior to all other imaging modalities and, because it detects fat and vascular spaces, offers an opportunity to subtype adenomas in up to 80% of cases (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). The French multisociety guidance adds that hepatobiliary contrast has additional value specifically for focal nodular hyperplasia.
standard.avoid: Do not accept an ultrasound or single-phase CT diagnosis and then counsel on it, and do not assume the diagnosis is secure because somebody resected it. In the multicentre prospective pregnancy cohort, 18 of 66 women (27%) referred with a suspected adenoma under 5 cm turned out to have focal nodular hyperplasia once hepatobiliary-contrast MRI was done — a lesion with no bleeding or malignant risk and no follow-up requirement at all. In the Dutch nationwide audit of 222 resections performed for a presumed adenoma, the postoperative diagnosis differed from the preoperative one in 43% of cases, rising to 70% of lesions under 50 mm and 78% of male patients; focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected sub-50 mm lesions. Independent predictors of a changed diagnosis were lesion under 50 mm (adjusted odds ratio 3.4), male sex (3.7) and absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI (1.8). In the Korean nationwide series of 121 patients with 138 adenomas, hepatocellular adenoma was not suspected at all in 31.6% of the original radiology reports.
standard.note: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound separates adenoma from focal nodular hyperplasia by the absence of the central spoke-wheel pattern, but EASL is explicit that it is not accurate enough to subtype an adenoma. Fix the measurement convention locally — longest axial diameter on the same sequence each time — because the growth trigger downstream is a 20% change. The Dutch audit is retrospective and selected on having been resected, so it cannot say how often the diagnosis is wrong in a lesion that was watched; the authors note it is plausibly worse, which would strengthen rather than weaken the point. The adjusted odds ratio of 1.8 for absence of hepatobiliary contrast is confounded by era and centre and should not be read as an effect of the agent alone.

opts.name: HNF1A-inactivated (H-HCA)
opts.when: EASL 2016: positive identification of HNF1A-inactivated adenoma is achievable with MRI with more than 90% specificity (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1).
opts.pref: The lesion with diffuse homogeneous signal dropout on chemical-shift opposed-phase T1, reflecting marked steatosis. Reported MRI sensitivity 87-91% and specificity 89-100% across two series of 50 and 44 adenomas. This is the subtype that lets you lengthen an interval: histological haemorrhage was the lowest of any subgroup at 39%, and no malignant transformation was seen in any HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman (0 of 47).
opts.avoid: Do not read any fatty adenoma as HNF1A-inactivated. Inflammatory adenomas that contain fat drop signal heterogeneously and moderately, and some HNF1A-inactivated adenomas are only mildly steatotic. Germline rather than somatic mutation in 8% of cases means a positive call should prompt a family and diabetes history.

opts.name: Inflammatory (I-HCA)
opts.when: EASL 2016 groups it with HNF1A-inactivated adenoma as identifiable by MRI with more than 90% specificity.
opts.pref: Strong T2 hyperintensity as bright as spleen, diffuse or as a peripheral rim (the atoll sign), with persistent enhancement on the delayed phase using extracellular contrast agents. Sensitivity 85-88%, specificity 88-100% with extracellular agents. Suspect it in obesity, metabolic syndrome or high alcohol intake, with a raised C-reactive protein, GGT and alkaline phosphatase; it is the least often symptomatic subtype at presentation (30%, P<0.0001).
opts.avoid: Do not use a hepatobiliary agent to make this call and expect the same numbers: with gadoxetic acid, sensitivity and specificity for inflammatory subtype fall to 80.9% and 77.3%, and nearly half of inflammatory adenomas are iso- or hyperintense on the hepatobiliary phase, mimicking focal nodular hyperplasia. About half of all beta-catenin-activated adenomas are also inflammatory, so an inflammatory phenotype does not exclude the high-risk driver.

opts.name: Beta-catenin-activated and unclassified
opts.when: EASL 2016 is explicit: identification of beta-catenin-activated adenoma, and its distinction from unclassified adenoma and from hepatocellular carcinoma, is not possible by any imaging technique (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1).
opts.pref: Nothing. If the subtype matters — and this is the subtype that matters most, carrying an odds ratio of 9.3 (95% CI 4.4-20.0) for malignant transformation — it needs tissue or it needs resecting. And tissue alone may not settle it: across 220 adenomas, 373 carcinomas and 17 borderline lesions, only 27% of the 33 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas tested showed the textbook strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern, so immunohistochemical triage under-detects the very subtype it is deployed to find, and those authors recommended mutation screening. The narrative review of the WHO 6th-edition classification says the same: nuclear beta-catenin staining has sensitivity too low to be reliable in routine practice, especially on a biopsy, glutamine synthetase is the usable surrogate, and every inflammatory adenoma should have glutamine synthetase staining to detect an added CTNNB1 mutation.
opts.avoid: Do not treat heterogeneous T2 signal with a central scar and no chemical-shift dropout as a beta-catenin diagnosis. Gadoxetic acid retention occurs in both inflammatory and beta-catenin adenomas and reflects OATP1B1/B3 expression, not the driver. Unclassified adenomas have no characteristic imaging feature at all.

opts.name: Sonic hedgehog (shHCA)
opts.when: Described after EASL 2016 and therefore absent from it: a subgroup defined by focal INHBE deletion producing an INHBE-GLI1 fusion, 22 of 533 adenomas (4%) in the reference series, previously counted as unclassified.
opts.pref: Suspect it rather than diagnose it: 100% female, higher BMI, and the only subgroup associated with symptomatic bleeding — 71% versus 14% in every other subgroup, P<0.0001. The obese woman who presents with a bled adenoma is the phenotype.
opts.avoid: Do not expect to find it on MRI; no imaging phenotype has been defined, and no reliable routine immunohistochemical marker exists either. Prostaglandin D synthase is specific but insensitive, and in the study that proposed it was diffusely positive in all 5 sonic hedgehog adenomas tested and negative in the others — a numerator of five. Argininosuccinate synthase 1 is sensitive and not specific: it was proposed as a marker of high bleeding risk but turns out to sit downstream of the INHBE-GLI1 fusion as part of a periportal expression programme, correlating with GLI1 at R=0.75 (P<0.0001), and ASS1 messenger RNA was not associated with histological haemorrhage at all. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states plainly that a reliable immunohistochemical marker for routine practice is still lacking and molecular profiling remains the gold standard. Do not use ASS1 as a bleeding-risk score.

standard.order: Ordered by how well imaging performs, not by how much each subtype matters — and the two are inverted. The two subtypes MRI identifies reliably are the two that change management least; the two that decide whether this patient needs an operation are the two imaging cannot call. That inversion is the single most important fact on this page, and the full-text read makes it worse rather than better: subtype accuracy does not deteriorate in small lesions (80% versus 87.5% below and above 5 cm, P=0.45), so the obstacle is not resolution but biology, and neither beta-catenin nor sonic hedgehog adenoma has a usable routine marker — only 27% of mutated adenomas show the glutamine synthetase pattern the algorithms key on, nuclear beta-catenin is too insensitive for a biopsy, prostaglandin D synthase is specific but insensitive and was assessed in 5 cases, and the review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that molecular profiling remains the reference standard.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item: does the programme commit to a standing four-antibody immunohistochemical panel (LFABP, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin, SAA or CRP) on every adenoma specimen and biopsy, with CTNNB1 sequencing reported by exon and codon where activation is suspected, and will prostaglandin D synthase be available for the sonic hedgehog subgroup? EASL 2016 says routine subtyping is not justified; the molecular data since, the Italian guideline's own biopsy recommendation, the WHO 6th-edition position that exon 3 adenomas are resected whatever their size, and the local transplant protocol's molecular route all assume it is available. The full-text read sharpens the question: immunohistochemistry alone missed 4 beta-catenin mutations that sequencing found in one male series, and only 27% of mutated adenomas show the textbook glutamine synthetase pattern — so a panel without sequencing will under-detect the subtype it is deployed to find. Registry: subtype assigned, method used, concordance with the resection specimen.

standard.t: Record whether the background liver is at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma, because that one fact decides which pathway this patient belongs on.
standard.pref: Cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, or current or prior hepatocellular carcinoma. Any of those and this is the HCC pathway from here, assessed on its own terms with LI-RADS and the OPTN imaging criteria; an adenoma in a cirrhotic liver is an unusual enough claim to need expert pathology before it is accepted. Absence of an at-risk background is the usual case and is the reason the HCC imaging criteria cannot be borrowed later.
standard.avoid: Do not carry an adenoma diagnosis forward without this line in the note. The local hepatic adenoma protocol builds its entire malignant-transformation routing on it: because most adenoma-derived carcinoma arises in a non-cirrhotic, non-at-risk liver, OPTN Class 5 classification and LI-RADS do not apply and the lesion cannot be classified on imaging alone.

alt.t: Biopsy when the imaging is atypical, when malignant transformation is suspected, or when the subtype will change what you do — and not otherwise.
alt.pref: EASL: biopsy may be considered within a benign liver tumour multidisciplinary team to exclude malignancy. ACG 2024: obtaining a biopsy should be reserved for cases in which imaging is inconclusive (strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline goes further and recommends biopsy wherever the subtype is not classifiable on imaging, specifically to identify beta-catenin exon 3 and sonic hedgehog adenomas, quoting major complications of image-guided liver biopsy at 0.1-4.6% and of adenoma biopsy specifically at no mortality, 2% major and 10% minor — but it grades that recommendation very low quality (D), conditional. The local hepatic adenoma protocol says the biopsy should target the dominant or most suspicious lesion. In 47 resected adenomas with both preoperative MRI and biopsy, biopsy subtyped correctly in 76.6% (95% CI 61-88) on morphology alone and 81.6% (65-93) where immunohistochemistry was available in 38 of 47, against 85.1% (71-94) for the senior blinded MRI reader and 76.6% (61-88) for the junior one, interobserver kappa 0.85 (0.69-0.97); the two agreed in 74.5% of cases and where they agreed the likelihood ratio for the subtype exceeded 20.
alt.avoid: Do not biopsy reflexively. EASL states plainly that there is no justification for recommending histopathology or molecular subtyping of adenoma as routine clinical practice, and do not biopsy a lesion you have already decided to resect — the resection specimen answers more questions than the needle and a negative needle will not stop the operation. The immunophenotypical markers add most in steatotic lesions and least where tissue is scant.
alt.note: Two findings in that series matter more than its headline. First, accuracy did not deteriorate in small lesions: for adenomas under 5 cm against those over 5 cm, imaging was correct in 80% versus 87.5% (P=0.45), routine biopsy 66.7% versus 81.3% (P=0.27) and biopsy with immunohistochemistry 75% versus 84.6% (P=0.48), and tumour size did not differ between correctly and incorrectly classified lesions (6.3 versus 6.8 cm, P=0.71) — which removes the main technical objection to subtype-based management of small lesions, and is reported in one sentence that the paper's own conclusion does not carry. Second, only three lesions in the whole series showed beta-catenin activation and none was analysed as a separate category, so the study does not establish that the subtype which should override size can be detected at all; 72% of its lesions were telangiectatic or inflammatory, far above the usual third, which inflates every accuracy figure. Both biopsy and MRI are also reference-standard-limited: truth was the resection specimen, so only lesions someone had decided to resect could enter.

alt.t: Where tissue exists, ask for the four-antibody panel, and for the CTNNB1 exon and codon when beta-catenin activation is in question.
alt.pref: LFABP, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin and SAA or CRP. In the 533-adenoma molecular series this panel reproduced the major molecular subtypes with sensitivity and specificity of 0.85 to 0.93 depending on the marker. Glutamine synthetase pattern carries real information: strong homogeneous staining goes with the highly activating exon 3 mutants, diffuse heterogeneous staining with a glutamine-synthetase-positive and CD34-negative rim with S45, and faint patchy staining with no nuclear beta-catenin with exon 7/8 alterations, which are not associated with increased malignant risk. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification sets out the same mapping, and adds that every inflammatory adenoma should be stained for glutamine synthetase because about one in ten carries an added CTNNB1 mutation that no other feature reveals.
alt.avoid: Do not treat immunohistochemistry as equivalent to sequencing. In the Dutch nationwide series of 66 male adenomas, next-generation sequencing identified 4 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas that neither immunohistochemistry nor expert re-review had found. Across the genotype-phenotype series, only 27% of the 33 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas tested showed the strong homogeneous pattern that the algorithms key on, and S45-mutated adenomas give an intense but heterogeneous pattern that the authors describe as difficult to recognise — their conclusion was that the immunohistochemical criteria must be revised or mutation screening performed. Nuclear beta-catenin has good specificity and insufficient sensitivity, because very few nuclei may stain.
alt.note: The exon and codon matter downstream: the local transplant protocol's molecular route turns on them, and S45 exon 3 is a genuinely contested category — see the honest section and the transplant gate. The classification itself began as three genotype-phenotype groups in 96 lesions, in which carcinoma or a borderline lesion was present in 46% of beta-catenin-mutated tumours and in none of the inflammatory ones (P=0.004); the eight-subgroup version and the immunohistochemical panel are refinements of that original observation.

avoid.t: Do not ablate or embolise a small indeterminate lesion before you know what it is.
avoid.pref: Biopsy it instead, which is EASL's explicit instruction: for smaller indeterminate lesions, ablation without confirmation of diagnosis is not recommended, and biopsy should be considered.
avoid.avoid: Ablation destroys the specimen, and the specimen is how malignant transformation is actually detected in this disease. A small lesion treated without a diagnosis leaves you with neither a diagnosis nor a follow-up rule.

avoid.t: Do not run an adenoma patient through imaging criteria that were not built for them.
avoid.pref: Use the adenoma phenotype described above, and state in the report which subtype criteria were applied and which were not assessable.
avoid.avoid: LI-RADS and OPTN Class 5 classification are defined for patients at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma. Applying them to a young woman with a normal liver generates a category that means nothing and, worse, generates a transplant-pathway assumption that the local protocol specifically corrects.

gates.name: 2 · Risk-factor modification, and how long you may wait
crit: Oestrogen-containing contraception, a hormone-containing intrauterine device, or any other oestrogen exposure
Anabolic-androgenic steroid or androgen therapy exposure, including non-prescribed use
Overweight, obesity, type 2 diabetes or other features of the metabolic syndrome
Alcohol intake of 30 g a day or more
A woman whose adenoma is not yet an indication for operation on size, growth, subtype or sex
gates.ask: Can this lesion be made smaller without an operation, and how long am I allowed to wait before I call that a failure?

standard.t: Stop oestrogen and androgen exposure, counsel on contraception and pregnancy, and put the advice in writing.
standard.pref: Every patient at diagnosis. EASL: upon adenoma diagnosis, lifestyle changes such as discontinuation of oral contraceptives as well as weight loss should be advised (evidence level II-2, grade of recommendation 1). ACG 2024 is firmer in wording and weaker in evidence: oral contraceptives, hormone-containing intrauterine devices and anabolic steroids are to be avoided (strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline is the only one that grades discontinuing oral contraceptives any higher than the rest of its adenoma recommendations — low quality (C) but strength 1, strong — while conceding that no randomised trial compares continuation with discontinuation and that the evidence is small case series. The exposure association is consistent, and recent hormone use within 6 months was independently associated with rupture in the 124-patient multicentre series (odds ratio 4.46, 95% CI 1.49-13.33), an effect of the same order as the size effect in the same model.
standard.avoid: Do not present withdrawal as sufficient, and do not promise it will be quick. In the three-centre US cohort of 187 to 193 patients, 69% showed regression after oral contraceptive cessation, but 47% of that cohort still had a lesion of 5 cm or more and haemorrhage occurred in 10 of 193 (5%) at a median lesion size of 8.7 cm. In the Dutch timing cohort, regression below 5 cm had occurred in only 8.5-15.3% of patients at 26 weeks. Hormone withdrawal also has no demonstrated effect on malignant transformation.
standard.note: Androgen exposure is not only prescribed. Non-prescribed anabolic steroid use in a man presenting with an adenoma should be asked about directly and recorded, because it clusters with the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype. Ask about alcohol in the same breath and record the quantity: in the 261-patient French multicentre bleeding cohort regular alcohol consumption carried an odds ratio of 9.16 (95% CI 2.47-34.01) for haemorrhage, nine times the effect of a centimetre of diameter, and in the 533-adenoma series alcohol was an independent predictor of malignant transformation at 4.85. Both are modifiable; neither has been pursued as an alternative to resection in any published series.

standard.t: Treat the weight, and treat it as a tumour intervention rather than as general advice.
standard.pref: Every overweight or obese patient, and every patient with an inflammatory-subtype adenoma. EASL recommends control of body weight alongside stopping oral contraceptives, and reports regression of tumour burden in up to a third of patients complying with lifestyle change, with progression associated with obesity. In the three-centre US cohort, 47% of patients had a lesion of 5 cm or more and 54 of them had adenomatosis, in a population in which metabolic disease was the dominant association. In the Taiwanese series of 45 adenomas, where only 3 women had ever taken oral contraceptives and 58% of patients were male, 75% of the adenomas were of the inflammatory subtype — so in a population without hormone exposure the metabolic driver is what is left.
standard.avoid: Do not promise regression, and do not count it as a treatment effect. The regression figures are uncontrolled before-and-after observations in cohorts where hormone withdrawal happened at the same time, so the weight effect cannot be isolated from the hormone effect — and the untreated comparator is not zero: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm fell below 5 cm with no intervention at all, at a median of 104 weeks. Any claimed effect of weight loss has to beat that, and none of the published series is designed to.
standard.note: Name an owner for the weight plan — bariatric medicine, endocrinology or primary care — the same way you would name an owner for a drain. An unassigned weight plan is the commonest reason a 6-month scan shows nothing has changed.

standard.t: Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months, and treat that scan as a trajectory rather than a verdict — six months is too early to call risk-factor modification a failure.
standard.pref: Every presumed adenoma. EASL advises reassessment with contrast-enhanced MRI after 6 months for all presumed adenomas, and in women a period of 6 months observation after lifestyle change (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2). ACG 2024 uses a looser 6- to 12-month interval and does not tie it to a size trigger (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline specifies MRI at 6 months after contraceptive discontinuation, repeat at 1 year if unchanged or reduced below 5 cm, and annual ultrasound after the first 18 months — and grades every one of those steps very low quality (D), conditional.
standard.avoid: Do not treat a lesion still over 5 cm at 6 months as a failed trial. In 194 patients with adenomas larger than 5 cm followed with serial imaging, regression to 5 cm or less had occurred in only 8.5-15.3% at 26 weeks — the exact point at which EASL and ACG advise resection — rising to 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks, with 69 of 118 (58.5%) regressing below 5 cm eventually at a median of 104 weeks (95% CI 80-128). Time to regression was strongly size-dependent: a median of 63 weeks for lesions under 7 cm, 109 weeks for 7-10 cm and 208 weeks for those over 10 cm (P<0.001). No complication occurred anywhere in that follow-up. A decision point at six months therefore identifies roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually fall below the line, which means the timing of the rule — not only the value of the threshold — drives resections that a longer wait would have avoided.
standard.note: Read against that, the counter-evidence is thin. The single-institution surgical series that reports no significant regression at six months does not define significant regression and did not look beyond six months, in a literature whose median time to regression is about two years — so the observation arm was never given a fair test before the surgical policy was validated against it. The Dutch cohort has its own problems: 47 of 241 patients were excluded for under six months of follow-up, which removes precisely the patients in whom the guideline rule was applied, and regression is defined as crossing the 5 cm line, so a lesion falling from 12 cm to 6 cm counts as a non-responder. EASL's growth trigger is a diameter increase of 20% or more, taken from RECIST 1.1, which was built for response assessment in solid malignancy and has never been validated in a benign liver lesion; on a 5 cm lesion it is 1 cm, small enough that the measurement convention in the radiology report decides whether the trigger fires.

alt.t: Extend observation past 12 months in a woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin adenoma that is shrinking.
alt.pref: The patient whose lesion is falling, whose risk factors are still being modified, and for whom the operation would be major. This is the conclusion the 194-patient cohort's own authors drew: the cut-off in women with typical, non-beta-catenin-activated adenoma could be prolonged to 12 months irrespective of baseline diameter. A PROSPERO-registered meta-analysis of 7 retrospective studies and 699 surveilled patients across Europe and the United States found 88.5% (95% CI 74.9-95.2) stable or regressed, with pooled symptomatic bleeding of 0.5% (95% CI 0.1-3.5) and pooled malignant transformation of 0.8% (95% CI 0.4-1.9) over median follow-up ranging from 2 to 5.8 years. Those two figures are one to two orders of magnitude below the historical references the 5 cm rule was built on — spontaneous bleeding of 20-40% and transformation of 4-10% — and the authors explain the gap: the founding cohorts were small surgical series of 6 to 30 cm lesions in which almost nothing was an incidental finding, and they did not separate histological from symptomatic bleeding. A contemporary 164-patient cohort managed 76.2% of its patients by surveillance and reports rupture in 1.8%, regression in 18.4% and no malignant transformation at all among those watched.
alt.avoid: Do not read 88.5% and 0.5% as the risk of watching any adenoma. In five of the seven pooled studies, lesions were pulled out of the surveillance group by intervention whenever they grew or looked worrying, so these are the outcomes of the lesions that were allowed to remain under observation and not of all adenomas over 5 cm — informative censoring that no random-effects model corrects. Six of the seven carried a moderate to serious risk of bias, their definitions of stability differed (RECIST in four, a 1 cm threshold, regression below 5 cm, or unspecified in the rest), and removing one outlying study moved pooled progression from 11.5% to 18.1%. The confidence interval for symptomatic bleeding runs from 0.1% to 3.5%, a thirty-five-fold range, so the headline figure is far more precise-sounding than the data support; the meta-analysis also overlaps substantially with the individual cohorts cited elsewhere on this page and is not independent of them. The 164-patient cohort has the same problem in a simpler form: zero transformation in a surveillance group chosen by clinicians who judged those lesions low-risk is the expected result of successful selection. Do not extend any of it to a man, a beta-catenin-activated or unclassified lesion, an exophytic lesion, or one that is growing.
alt.note: EASL's own later intervals, for the lesion that stabilises: stable after 12 months, annual imaging is acceptable; stable or reducing after 5 years, biannual imaging can be proposed; ultrasound is cost-effective and may be preferred for a well-seen lesion. EASL also says there is no robust data on the timeline that defines stable disease. A 2026 narrative review of nonoperative management reaches the same direction of travel — that recent data support extending non-operative management even to lesions over 5 cm, because they can respond to lifestyle intervention — but it is a review of the same retrospective cohorts and adds no new comparative data.

alt.t: Where the subtype is known and low risk, let it lengthen the interval rather than shorten the operating list.
alt.pref: A confidently subtyped HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman. EASL notes that subtyping may be used in some specialist centres to support longer intervals between imaging follow-up, and the molecular series found no malignant transformation in any HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman (0 of 47). The usual technical objection — that subtyping is unreliable in small lesions — is not supported: in the series that measured it, subtype accuracy was 80% below 5 cm against 87.5% above (P=0.45) for imaging and 75% against 84.6% (P=0.48) for biopsy with immunohistochemistry, and lesion size did not differ between correctly and incorrectly classified lesions.
alt.avoid: Do not let a reassuring subtype override size, growth, male sex or an exophytic position, and do not let an unreassuring subtype alone commit a patient to an operation that size and growth do not justify. EASL states that whether the haemorrhage or malignant-transformation risk attributed to beta-catenin activation is independent of sex, size and rate of change is presently unknown, and that prospective validation of imaging-based subtyping is necessary before widespread implementation. The 0 of 47 figure is also a resection-series denominator and is small: it excludes nothing above a few per cent.
alt.note: This asymmetry — subtype may reassure but may not alone commit — is a local safety convention, not a guideline position. It is in the honest section for that reason.

avoid.t: Do not accept lifestyle advice as the whole plan in a man, in a proven beta-catenin-activated adenoma, or in a lesion that is growing.
avoid.pref: Those three go to the resection gate. EASL recommends resection irrespective of size in men and in any instance of proven beta-catenin mutation (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2).
avoid.avoid: Hormone withdrawal has no demonstrated effect on malignant transformation, and in men the associated condition driving transformation since 2000 has been the metabolic syndrome rather than hormone exposure — so there may be no hormone to withdraw.

avoid.t: Do not operate on a large adenoma at 6 months without telling the patient what waiting another six months would probably have done.
avoid.pref: Document the conversation: only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm had fallen below 5 cm at 26 weeks against 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks, no complication occurred during that follow-up, and the counter-argument is a surgical series' selection bias rather than a measured hazard of waiting.
avoid.avoid: This is where practice diverges most from the written guideline. In a European expert survey, 48 of 61 analysable respondents (79%) advise against routine resection of a hepatocellular adenoma larger than 5 cm after lifestyle change — a direct majority rejection of the EASL recommendation — and only 31 of 61 (51%) reported having an EASL-compliant benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary team. Read it with its limits: 61 of 294 invited clinicians responded (21%), the respondents are self-selected specialists at referral centres, and the survey records stated advice rather than observed practice — the same group's own national audit found 20% of resections for presumed adenoma were performed on lesions under 50 mm. Do not pretend the question is closed in either direction.

gates.name: 3 · Male sex — the independent indication
crit: Male patient with a hepatocellular adenoma of any size
Androgen or anabolic-steroid exposure, current or past
Nuclear beta-catenin or strong diffuse glutamine synthetase staining, or a confirmed CTNNB1 mutation
Cellular atypia, pseudoglandular formation or cholestasis on biopsy
A diagnosis of adenoma made outside an expert liver pathology service
gates.ask: This is a man with an adenoma — what is the chance there is already carcinoma in it?

standard.t: Resect, irrespective of size, and treat the lesion as possibly already malignant rather than as a benign tumour with a future risk.
standard.pref: Every male adenoma. EASL: resection or curative treatment is recommended for all adenomas diagnosed in men because of a significantly higher incidence of malignant transformation, irrespective of size (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2); the Italian multisociety guideline says the same at very low quality of evidence (D), conditional. In the 218-patient tertiary series malignant transformation occurred in 4% of women and 47% of men; beta-catenin activation was present in 16 of the 25 transformed adenomas (64%). In the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French surgical series malignant transformation was about ten-fold more frequent in men than in women. In the 533-adenoma molecular series male sex was the second strongest independent predictor of transformation at an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2), behind only TERT promoter mutation.
standard.avoid: Do not be reassured by a small adenoma in a man, and do not overstate what the evidence for the rule is. The transformed adenomas in the 218-patient series had a median diameter of 10 cm and only 3 of 25 were 5 cm or smaller — and all three of those arose in a liver with fibrosis or iron overload, which argues for the background liver rather than for size. In the 122-patient series the one malignancy under 5 cm was in a man taking steroids, so that paper's own data are consistent with size being irrelevant once sex and androgen exposure are accounted for. Sex and size are therefore not independent in any of the published data, and the irrespective of size rule rests on the sex effect rather than on any observed outcome in small male lesions.
standard.note: Metabolic syndrome, not hormone exposure, has been the commonest associated condition in men with malignant transformation since 2000, and the number of such men has risen markedly over that period. Androgen exposure concentrated in beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas with or without inflammation (P<0.0001) in the 411-patient molecular series. The male series are small and selected: the 218-patient cohort is a tertiary surgical series in which men with large or suspicious lesions are preferentially referred and operated, so 47% is close to a maximum rather than a population risk, and the finding that half of presumed male adenomas are not adenomas on expert review means part of that 47% may be misclassification of carcinoma as transformed adenoma. The rule may well be right; the number behind it is not a risk estimate. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review, with sequencing, before you accept the diagnosis.
standard.pref: Every male case, including those referred with an outside diagnosis. In the Dutch nationwide series of 66 men from 26 centres, the diagnosis changed after expert revision plus next-generation sequencing in 33 of 66 (50%): the final diagnoses were 20 adenoma, 26 lesion of uncertain malignant potential and 20 hepatocellular carcinoma. Tumour-related mortality tracked the revised diagnosis — 1 of 18 (5.6%) for adenoma, 5 of 14 (35.7%) for uncertain malignant potential and 4 of 9 (44.4%) for carcinoma (P=0.031). The full malignancy panel of glutamine synthetase, glypican-3 and HSP70 had been performed primarily in only 8 of 66 cases (12%), rising to 55 of 66 (83%) after revision. The Dutch resection audit found the same thing prospectively from the other end: male sex independently predicted a change of diagnosis after resection (adjusted odds ratio 3.7), and 78% of male patients resected for a presumed adenoma had their diagnosis changed.
standard.avoid: Do not rely on immunohistochemistry alone: sequencing in that series found 4 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas that neither immunohistochemistry nor expert re-review had identified. The authors' own conclusion was that sequencing may be more important for subtyping than current guidelines indicate.
standard.note: That 50% reclassification figure comes from a registry-based pathology review with no comparator, selected on the availability of tissue, and is as much a statement about the difficulty of the distinction as about outside laboratories. Note also that the mortality denominators (18, 14 and 9) do not match the final diagnostic groups (20, 26 and 20), so a substantial fraction of patients lacked follow-up and the direction of that loss is not stated; and that only 12% had the standard malignancy panel done originally, which means the pre-revision cohort is not a fair comparator for the post-revision one. The distinction being made — adenoma against well-differentiated carcinoma in a non-cirrhotic liver — is one of the hardest in liver pathology.

opts.name: Resection
opts.when: EASL, ACG 2024 and the Italian 2022 guideline all say resect a male adenoma — the Italian one at very low quality of evidence (D), conditional. The Brazilian surgical series adopted the same rule after using a 4 cm threshold and then a 5 cm threshold in earlier eras, which is itself worth noticing: one institution ran three different cut-offs over one study period, each adopted without new local data, and reported comparable outcomes under all three.
opts.pref: Any male patient fit for the operation. It is the only option that produces a specimen, which is how transformation in men is actually detected. In the 134-patient Brazilian series, 124 resections gave 8.1% morbidity and no mortality; malignant transformation was found in 4 of 124 (3.2%), all beta-catenin-activated and all larger than 5 cm. Parenchyma-sparing and laparoscopic approaches should be the default in a young patient with benign disease.
opts.avoid: Do not accept a major hepatectomy without asking whether a parenchyma-sparing resection reaches the same lesion. These are young patients and the indication is benign in most of them. And do not quote the 8.1% morbidity as reassurance without saying that it is reported with no Clavien-Dindo distribution, so the clinical weight of those complications is unknown.

opts.name: Observation with a sequenced, confidently low-risk subtype
opts.when: Not a guideline position. EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all recommend resection in men irrespective of size.
opts.pref: A man with a small, hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed, sequenced HNF1A-inactivated adenoma with no CTNNB1 alteration, who is a poor operative candidate and accepts close surveillance with a documented reason. There is no cohort that supports this. The full-text read of the male series found no followed, biopsy-only male cohort to cite: what exists is 4 malignant transformations in 27 male adenomas (14.8%), occurring in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions, with androgen receptor staining positive in half of cases and not associated with transformation.
opts.avoid: Half of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert review, 78% of male resections in the national audit had their diagnosis changed, and transformation in the male pathology series occurred in unclassified as well as beta-catenin lesions — so a subtype-only reassurance in a man is reassurance about a label that is frequently wrong, assigned by a method that misses mutations sequencing finds. Do not offer this as an equivalent option, and do not offer it at all without sequencing and a board decision.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: No male-specific data exist. EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates.
opts.pref: A small, accessible lesion in a prohibitive operative candidate in whom tissue has already established the subtype and excluded atypia.
opts.avoid: Ablation destroys the specimen, and the specimen is how malignant transformation in men is found. Do not ablate a male adenoma you have not biopsied, and record that the trade-off was explained.

alt.order: Ordered as every guideline orders it, on the strength of a roughly ten-fold difference in malignancy prevalence between the sexes in retrospective surgical series — 47% against 4% in the largest, with male sex an independent predictor at an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2) in the molecular series. There is no randomised, and no matched, comparison of resection against observation in male adenoma, and there will not be one. The full-text read adds a complication the guidelines do not address: the diagnostic label is unreliable in exactly this group, with half of presumed male adenomas reclassified on expert review and 78% of male resections having their diagnosis changed, so part of the apparent sex effect may be misclassification of carcinoma as transformed adenoma.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: does the programme resect every male adenoma irrespective of size, as EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all state, or will it accept documented observation for a sequenced, subtyped, small HNF1A-inactivated lesion in a poor operative candidate? Correction: the earlier draft of this page framed this question around two figures — 23.8% occult carcinoma in male resections, and no transformation in 7 biopsied lesions followed for a mean 5 years — and the full-text read supports neither. The supported figures are malignant transformation in 4 of 27 male adenomas (14.8%), occurring in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions, with androgen receptor staining positive in half of cases and not associated with transformation; and no cohort anywhere of observed, biopsy-only male adenomas. So the observation option currently has no supporting data at all, and the group should decide whether it is prepared to offer something on that basis. Registry: sex, size, subtype, immunohistochemistry and sequencing results, decision, specimen finding, and the explant or specimen concordance with the preoperative diagnosis.

alt.t: Where an androgen exposure can be stopped, stop it — but do not wait on it before operating.
alt.pref: Anabolic steroid use for sport or bodybuilding, androgen therapy for aplastic anaemia or paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, and endogenous androgen excess. EASL links the rising male incidence to these exposures, and androgen exposure clusters with the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype.
alt.avoid: There is no regression series for androgen withdrawal comparable to the oral-contraceptive data, and the 6-month observation window EASL grants to women is explicitly not extended to men. Stopping the androgen is harm reduction, not treatment.

avoid.t: Do not use a normal alpha-fetoprotein to exclude carcinoma in a male adenoma.
avoid.pref: Measure it where transformation is a concern, record it, and treat an elevated value as informative in one direction only. The ACMG glycogen storage disease guideline states the same conclusion for a different population: alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen do not predict malignant transformation and cannot be used for surveillance.
avoid.avoid: The local hepatic adenoma protocol states the rule explicitly: alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude carcinoma when normal. In the male series the discriminating test was expert pathology plus sequencing, not a serum marker.

avoid.t: Do not treat an androgen-exposed adenoma as though it were an oestrogen-exposed one.
avoid.pref: Record the exposure, expect the beta-catenin exon 3 subtype, and send for sequencing.
avoid.avoid: The 6-month lifestyle-modification window, the 5 cm threshold and the expectation of regression all come from cohorts that were 85 to 99% female. None of them has been tested in androgen-driven disease, and the one series that reported both sexes found malignant transformation in 47% of men against 4% of women.

gates.name: 4 · Size and growth — the 5 cm convention, and which intervention
crit: Adenoma still larger than 5 cm after an adequate trial of risk-factor modification — and an explicit note of how long that trial has run, because six months is too early
Diameter increase of 20% or more on comparable imaging — EASL's RECIST-based growth trigger, never validated in a benign liver lesion
Exophytic protrusion from the liver surface, or lesional arteries visible on imaging
Lesion in segment II or III
Symptoms attributable to the lesion
Subtype, where it is known — a beta-catenin exon 3 or sonic hedgehog result changes the decision more than a centimetre of diameter does
gates.ask: Has this lesion's size or growth earned an operation yet — and does the patient know that 5 cm is a convention rather than a measured threshold?

standard.t: Treat a lesion that is persistently larger than 5 cm, or growing by 20% or more, as an indication for curative treatment — and say plainly, to the patient and in the note, that 5 cm is a convention and not a derived threshold.
standard.pref: EASL: adenomas persistently greater than 5 cm, or increasing in size by 20% or more of diameter as per RECIST, should be considered for resection or curative treatment irrespective of their molecular or histological subtype, because of the risk of haemorrhage; in women resection is indicated for nodules equal to or greater than 5 cm and those continuing to grow (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2). ACG 2024 agrees that lesions of 5 cm or more warrant intervention because of rupture and malignancy risk (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). The recommendation stands on this page. What has changed is how it should be described.
standard.avoid: Do not present the number as derived, because it is not, and every document that states it says so in its own grading. EASL calls it the accepted clinically relevant size cut off — accepted, not derived — and supports its central factual premise, that in nearly all cases of spontaneous rupture or haemorrhage the lesion is at least 5 cm, with a single citation; it grades the recommendation at evidence level II-3, non-randomised observational evidence, with recommendation strength 2, its weaker category. The Italian multisociety guideline is the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework with PICO questions, QUADAS-2 and ROBINS-I appraisal and formal voting, and it grades every size-based adenoma recommendation — the 5 cm resection trigger, the resect-all-men rule, the 6-month decision point and the whole surveillance schedule — as very low quality of evidence (D) with strength of recommendation 2, conditional. Where the threshold has been tested directly it has not held: in 261 patients with full molecular subtyping, diameter was modelled continuously and acted as an independent risk factor for bleeding at an odds ratio of only 1.02 per millimetre (95% CI 1.01-1.03, P<0.001), with the authors stating that they did not identify a threshold size; the one study that set out to derive a bleeding cut-point derived 35 mm, not 50 mm; and the series usually cited for the rule fitted its own cut-point at 7 cm and recommended resecting above 4 cm. Do not apply the threshold before the risk-factor trial has run for long enough to mean anything, and do not apply it to a 5.2 cm lesion that has fallen from 8 cm without saying so to the patient.
standard.note: Graded D here rather than C, and the downgrade is the point: this is a consensus threshold that nobody derived, so it cannot be graded from the design of the cohorts that happen to be consistent with it. Four fifths of responding European experts decline to follow it, and one institution in the published literature ran 4 cm, then 5 cm, then a subtype-and-sex rule across a single study period with comparable outcomes under all three. Keeping the recommendation while grading it D is deliberate: the alternative on offer — subtype-directed management — requires tissue and sequencing that EASL declines to recommend routinely, so a programme cannot simply swap one rule for the other. What it can do is stop describing 5 cm as a risk threshold.

standard.t: State where the 5 cm number comes from, and record the position and vascularity of the lesion alongside its diameter.
standard.pref: Where the number comes from, said plainly. Three surgical datasets, none of them a test of a threshold. A systematic review of 28 articles and 1,176 patients reported haemorrhage in 315 of 1,160 patients (27.2%) but in only 118 of 748 lesions (15.8%), rupture in 114 of 651 (17.5%), and haemorrhage as the first symptom in 126 of 184 bleeding cases (68.5%); 1,073 of the 1,176 pooled patients (91.2%) had been resected, and the authors explicitly label their figures maximum risks for that reason. A 5-centre series of 124 patients found rupture in 31 (25%) and fitted its size dichotomy at 7 cm, not 5 cm — odds ratio 7.78 (95% CI 2.22-26.32) — alongside recent hormone use at 4.46 (1.49-13.33); malignancy was present in 5 patients (4%) and the smallest malignant adenoma measured 8 cm; the authors then recommended resecting adenomas larger than 4 cm, so three different numbers appear in one paper and the one that entered the guidelines has the least statistical support. A pooled review of 1,635 adenomas gave malignant transformation in 68 (4.2%) overall, 50 of 1,617 (3.1%) in series and 4.5% of the 1,462 resected, with only 3 of the 68 transformations (4.4%) in a tumour under 5 cm and the smallest transformed adenoma in the literature measuring 4 cm.
standard.avoid: Read each of those backwards before using it. Every one is a surgical series, so the denominators are patients selected for operation. The per-patient figure (27.2%) and the per-lesion figure (15.8%) differ by nearly twofold, which means a rule derived from per-lesion data and applied per patient is not the same rule — and most citations do not say which they mean. Two thirds of bleeds were the presenting event, so most haemorrhage is unpreventable by surveillance at any threshold. Six of the 13 articles in the systematic review that reported lesion size reported haemorrhage below 5 cm, and the smallest bled lesion in that literature measured 1 cm. The '4.4% below 5 cm' statistic is a proportion of the numerator, not a risk: it says nothing about the probability that a sub-5 cm adenoma transforms, and it is partly a function of how few sub-5 cm adenomas were in the pooled denominator at all, since 89% of the pooled lesions were resected and small lesions generally are not. In the one cohort assembled to derive a bleeding threshold, 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm bled (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above it (53%, P<0.001) — but that institution's own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected and therefore sectioned, no beta-catenin-activated adenoma was identified in the whole 195-lesion series and 48% were unclassifiable, so it cannot exclude subtype as the real driver of its apparent size effect. In the most favourable modern dataset, haemorrhage occurred in 13% of patients with a lesion of 5 cm or more against 0% below — but on 10 events at a median bleeding size of 8.7 cm, and a zero rate in roughly a hundred patients has an upper 95% bound of about 3%, so the data are compatible with a modest rather than an absent risk below 5 cm and support a cut-point well above 5 cm as readily as 5 cm itself.
standard.note: The direct tests of the threshold, in one place. In 533 adenomas the 50 mm cut-off separated histological haemorrhage (65% versus 40%, P<0.0001) but did not separate symptomatic bleeding (P=0.29) — and symptomatic bleeding is the outcome the operation is meant to prevent; the malignancy difference did not reach significance either (13.1% versus 7.6%, P=0.053). In 261 patients with full subtyping, size acted continuously at an odds ratio of 1.02 per millimetre (1.01-1.03), roughly a 1.2-fold increase in odds per centimetre, and no threshold could be identified, while sonic hedgehog subtype carried 21.02 (5.05-87.52), regular alcohol 9.16 (2.47-34.01) and beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 (1.78-23.55); body-mass index was not associated (P=0.71), and bleeding occurred below 5 cm. The apparently clean size gradient in the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French series — microscopic haemorrhage 0.9%, 19% and 68% and macroscopic 0%, 5% and 24% across the under-2 cm, 2-5 cm and over-5 cm strata — is largely an artefact of the denominator: that series was run under a policy of systematic resection, the sub-2 cm stratum consists almost entirely of incidental microadenomas found inside specimens removed for a different and larger lesion, and the over-5 cm stratum consists of the lesions that prompted the operation, so the two strata are not comparable populations. Counting 365 lesions in 122 patients inflates the small-lesion denominator mechanically, and microscopic haemorrhage found only because the specimen was removed and sectioned is an endpoint that cannot occur in a lesion left in situ. The 124-patient series' own authors recommended operating on asymptomatic adenomas approaching 4 cm; no guideline adopted it.

opts.name: Resection
opts.when: EASL: the recommended first-line therapy is resection of larger (over 5 cm) or growing lesions, aiming to remove the whole tumour and all risk of malignant transformation.
opts.pref: Unilobar or peripherally placed disease in a fit patient, and any lesion where malignant transformation is a live question — resection is the only option that yields a specimen. In a 134-patient single-centre series, 124 resections gave 8.1% morbidity and no mortality, with malignant transformation found in 4 (3.2%), all beta-catenin-activated and all larger than 5 cm. Parenchyma-sparing and laparoscopic approaches should be the default in a young patient with benign disease; the Italian multisociety guideline grades laparoscopic over open resection at low quality of evidence (C), conditional, on the strength of a Dutch nationwide comparison of 415 resections for benign tumours (59% of them adenoma) in which laparoscopy gave a shorter stay and lower morbidity after propensity matching.
opts.avoid: Do not accept a major hepatectomy for a lesion that is still shrinking on risk-factor modification, and do not resect a small indeterminate lesion when a biopsy would answer the question first. A fifth of the resections in the Dutch nationwide audit were performed on lesions under 50 mm, 70% of those had their diagnosis changed afterwards and 21% proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia — so the cost of operating early is measurable, and it is measured in operations on lesions that needed nothing.

opts.name: Transarterial embolisation
opts.when: EASL positions embolisation for larger lesions as an alternative to resection, but as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates.
opts.pref: A large, central or bilobar lesion for which the resection would be major, and the patient who wants to avoid an operation and accepts imaging follow-up afterwards. In the 59-patient cohort the median diameter fell from 76 mm to 48 mm by 5.5 months (P<0.001) and to 45 mm at 27.4 months. In a systematic review covering a pooled literature of 851 patients, 151 of whom had been embolised, surgery was avoided in 41 of 49 electively embolised patients (84%) and in 68 of 151 overall (45%), over a pooled median follow-up of 31 months.
opts.avoid: This is the option whose harms the page previously understated. In the 59-patient cohort, Society of Interventional Radiology grade D complications occurred in 6 patients (10%), one patient died three months after embolisation, and 20 of 59 (34%) ultimately required surgery anyway — so embolisation often adds a procedure rather than replacing one. Major complications occurred in 8 of 151 (5.3%) in the systematic review, pooled across emergency and elective indications, so the elective risk is not separately reported. Symptoms were unchanged after embolisation (P=0.134), so do not offer it for pain: it shrank lesions without relieving the complaint. A median post-treatment diameter of 45 mm means the typical embolised lesion sits just below the threshold rather than being eliminated, and the patient re-enters surveillance with an indeterminate lesion and no histology. 'Surgery avoided' is a process endpoint, not a patient outcome, and 31 months is too short to detect malignant transformation. EASL makes residual viable lesion on follow-up imaging an indication for resection.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: EASL positions ablation for smaller lesions as an alternative to resection and as the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates, and explicitly does not recommend ablation of a smaller indeterminate lesion without a confirmed diagnosis.
opts.pref: A small number of small, accessible lesions with the diagnosis already established, particularly where the alternative is a major resection. A stereotactic multiprobe series of 14 patients and 38 adenomas achieved technical efficacy in 97.4% with no major complications across 18 sessions, over a median follow-up of 49.6 months, with disease-free survival of 100% at the first time point and 85.8% thereafter.
opts.avoid: Conventional single-probe results are far weaker: in 18 patients and 45 adenomas, primary technical efficacy was achieved in only 26 of 45 (57.8%), and it depended entirely on approach — 79% for open ablation against 31% percutaneously (P=0.013), so the minimally invasive route, the only one that offers an advantage over surgery, failed two times in three. Two major complications occurred in those 18 patients. The stereotactic series is 14 patients at a single specialised centre whose senior author consults for the manufacturer of the navigation platform the technique depends on; a zero complication count in 18 sessions has an upper 95% bound of around 15%, and both series report per-lesion efficacy in patients with multiple nodules, which inflates the denominator. Neither provides tissue, so neither the diagnosis nor the exclusion of a malignant focus is established, and no study compares ablation with resection in this disease.

opts.name: Continued surveillance
opts.when: Not EASL's position for a lesion persistently over 5 cm, but the position the newer surveillance data support in a selected woman — and the position four fifths of responding European experts say they already take.
opts.pref: A woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin, hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed adenoma that is falling, where the operation would be major and the risk factors are still being addressed. Only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have fallen below 5 cm at 26 weeks, against 58.5% eventually at a median of 104 weeks, with no complication documented anywhere in that follow-up — so the six-month trigger is the wrong time to decide. The pooled contemporary surveillance figures are 88.5% stable or regressed (95% CI 74.9-95.2), symptomatic bleeding 0.5% (0.1-3.5) and malignant transformation 0.8% (0.4-1.9); in a 164-patient contemporary cohort, 76.2% were managed by surveillance with rupture in 1.8% and no malignant transformation among those watched.
opts.avoid: Do not extend it to a man, a beta-catenin-activated or unclassified lesion, an exophytic lesion, a lesion with visible arteries, a growing lesion, or a woman who wants to conceive now. The pooled figures come from cohorts already selected as safe to watch, and in five of the seven pooled studies lesions were removed from the surveillance group by intervention as soon as they grew — so the figures describe the lesions that were allowed to stay under observation, not all adenomas over 5 cm.

standard.order: Ordered as EASL orders them — resection first line, the non-surgical modalities as alternatives reserved for poor surgical candidates. That order reflects the guideline's wording and the fact that only resection yields a specimen. It does not reflect a demonstrated survival, bleeding or complication advantage, because no study compares any two of these four in hepatocellular adenoma. What the full-text read does establish about the alternatives is mostly cautionary: embolisation left 34% of patients still requiring surgery, caused one reported death and did not change symptoms (P=0.134); conventional ablation achieved primary efficacy in only 57.8% of lesions and 31% percutaneously; neither provides tissue; and continued surveillance, the option EASL does not endorse above 5 cm, now has the largest supporting dataset of the four.
standard.flagnote: Two ratification items. First: will the programme accept elective embolisation as a first-line alternative to resection in a good surgical candidate who prefers it? EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The 84% elective surgery-avoidance figure rests on 49 patients from multiple small series with no common protocol, and against it sit 10% grade D complications, one reported death three months after the procedure, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, unchanged symptoms at 3 months, no histology, and a pooled follow-up too short to detect transformation — a genuine shared decision, but one the page should not make quietly. Second: does the programme adopt a composite trigger — 5 cm, or growth of 20%, or exophytic position, or visible lesional arteries, or a segment II-III location — in place of diameter alone? Correction: the earlier draft asserted that the position and vascularity effects came out larger than diameter in one cohort. Those effect sizes could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn, so this item cannot be decided until someone reads that paper's positional analysis directly; what the paper does establish is a fitted cut-point at 35 mm. Registry: modality chosen, diameter change, complication by Clavien-Dindo grade, subsequent intervention, specimen or explant finding.

alt.t: Where the resection would be major and obesity is driving the disease, put bariatric referral on the table before the hepatectomy rather than after it.
alt.pref: The severely obese patient with multiple or large adenomas who is not bleeding and has time. In a three-patient series, body-mass index fell by 31-48% after bariatric surgery and two of the three showed complete regression of the adenoma without any liver-directed intervention. In a pooled review of 4 studies and 7 patients, body-mass index fell from a mean of 41 to 28 (P=0.002) and percentage excess weight loss correlated with reduction in the number of lesions (Spearman rho 0.78, P=0.04) but not significantly with reduction in lesion size (rho 0.46, P=0.29).
alt.avoid: Three patients and seven patients, all female, with no comparator and no adjustment for simultaneous hormone withdrawal — and formal correlation testing on seven patients is one observation away from non-significance. The positive finding concerns lesion number; the negative one concerns lesion size, which is the variable every threshold is built on, so the headline does not touch the decision variable. Both are published because the outcome was favourable; a series of non-responders would not have been written up. And the untreated comparator is not zero: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm regress below 5 cm with no intervention at all, so any claimed effect of weight loss has to beat that, and none of these studies is designed to. Do not describe bariatric surgery as a treatment for adenoma; describe it as treatment for the driver, with adenoma regression as a plausible consequence observed in single figures of patients.
alt.note: The same logic applies without an operation: the point is sustained weight loss, by whatever route the patient and the bariatric service agree on.

alt.t: Where a woman's adenoma sits between 4 and 5 cm, treat the decision as a judgement about subtype, position and trajectory rather than as a threshold.
alt.pref: The 4.5 cm exophytic lesion in segment III in a woman who wants to conceive, and equally the 4.5 cm lesion with a beta-catenin exon 3 result. Two findings bear on this band directly. First, the only cohort assembled to derive a bleeding cut-point derived 35 mm, with bleeding in 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above (53%, P<0.001) — so the band sits above, not below, the only empirically fitted threshold in the literature. Second, in a 164-patient contemporary cohort the 4-5 cm band comprised 26.8% of patients and 22.7% of them regressed, which is the most directly useful datum for this decision and rests on about 11 of 44 patients. Against both, the review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size, and that sonic hedgehog adenomas carry a high risk of haemorrhage even below 5 cm.
alt.avoid: No guideline endorses operating below 5 cm on position alone. The 35 mm cohort is retrospective, from one centre whose own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected, pooled trivial intratumoral blood with peritoneal rupture in its headline comparison, and identified no beta-catenin-activated adenoma at all in 195 lesions with 48% unclassifiable — so it cannot exclude subtype as the real driver. The WHO-review statements are expert assertion: the review cites no cohort quantifying either the exon 3 size-independence or the sub-5 cm sonic hedgehog bleeding risk, and concedes that the markers needed to identify both subtypes are insensitive, non-specific or available only by sequencing. Record the reasoning, present it as a judgement, and take it to the board rather than making it alone.
alt.note: The earlier draft of this page quoted exophytic position, visible lesional arteries and a segment II-III location with specific effect sizes attributed to the 35 mm cohort. Those specific figures were not carried in the full-text abstraction of that paper and could not be confirmed here, so they have been removed rather than restated; the composite-trigger proposal that rested on them remains in the honest section and in approval item 7 as a proposal, now graded D, pending someone reading that paper's positional analysis directly.

avoid.t: Do not report a small focus of haemorrhage inside an adenoma as an indication to operate.
avoid.pref: Record it, and let size, growth, subtype and sex make the decision.
avoid.avoid: EASL: small foci of haemorrhage within adenomas are often observed and are not an indication for clinical intervention (case series, evidence level 4). Histological bleeding was present in 52% of 533 adenomas while only 14% of patients presented with symptomatic bleeding, so incidental intralesional blood is the rule rather than a warning.

avoid.t: Do not use a reassuring subtype to withhold curative treatment from a lesion that is persistently over 5 cm or growing.
avoid.pref: Let the subtype lengthen the interval in a lesion below the threshold; once the threshold is crossed, EASL's rule is explicit that it applies irrespective of molecular or histological subtype, because the indication at that point is haemorrhage, not transformation. Note that the WHO 6th-edition classification, as reviewed in 2026, points the other way for one subtype: it states that beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size, which is a size-independent recommendation in the opposite direction — towards treating below 5 cm, not withholding above it.
avoid.avoid: The subtype data stratify malignant transformation well and bleeding less well, but not as poorly as the earlier draft of this page implied. In the 261-patient multivariate bleeding model, sonic hedgehog subtype carried an odds ratio of 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52) and beta-catenin exon 7/8 — the subtype with no increased malignant risk — carried 6.47 (1.78-23.55), against 1.02 per millimetre for diameter. Those confidence intervals are desperately wide and rest on a handful of events, so they identify the right axis without quantifying it usably. The practical problem is availability: sonic hedgehog subtype, the dominant bleeding predictor, cannot be identified on imaging and in practice requires sequencing, so the single most actionable bleeding predictor in the literature is not available in the clinic where the 5 cm decision is made.

gates.name: 5 · Acute haemorrhage and rupture
crit: Sudden severe upper abdominal pain in a patient with a known or suspected adenoma
Haemodynamic instability, or a falling haemoglobin
Intrahepatic or intraperitoneal haemorrhage on contrast-enhanced CT
Pregnancy or the early puerperium
An exophytic adenoma, or one 5 cm or larger
gates.ask: Do I stop the bleeding by embolising, and what do I owe this patient afterwards?

standard.t: Resuscitate with blood products, get a contrast-enhanced CT, and transfer to a centre that can embolise — embolisation, not resection, is the first manoeuvre in the unstable patient.
standard.pref: Haemodynamic instability with imaging evidence of active bleeding. EASL: a bleeding adenoma with haemodynamic instability should be embolised (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2); in cases of major haemorrhage, resuscitation with blood products and transfer to a centre where embolisation can be performed to control active bleeding is appropriate.
standard.avoid: Emergency major hepatectomy in a shocked young patient with a benign tumour. The review that proposed the acute algorithm makes the same point: standard treatment was surgical resection for both ruptured and unruptured tumours, and the shift to initial conservative management with selective embolisation is the change of the last fifteen years.
standard.note: Grade D by construction. There is no comparative series of embolisation against emergency resection in ruptured adenoma, and EASL's own grade for this recommendation is evidence level III. It is a sequence convention built on physiology and case series, and the page should not imply more. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Admit and observe the stable patient with contained haemorrhage, and do not operate in the acute phase.
standard.pref: Contained intralesional or intrahepatic bleeding with stable observations. EASL: if clinically evident haemorrhage occurs, admission for close observation and contrast-enhanced CT is appropriate. Operating on a freshly bled adenoma takes more parenchyma than the same operation six weeks later and makes the pathology harder to read.
standard.avoid: Do not discharge on the strength of a stable haemoglobin without a named owner, an interval scan and a plan to exclude malignancy.

standard.t: Re-image once stable, and treat residual viable lesion as an indication to resect.
standard.pref: Every patient who has bled. EASL: residual viable lesion on follow-up imaging is an indication for resection (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2), and further investigation once stable should be pursued to exclude malignancy and secure appropriate follow-up. In the systematic review of 851 patients, surgery was avoided altogether in 68 of 151 embolised patients (45%), so a substantial proportion need no second procedure — but that proportion is identified by re-imaging, not assumed.
standard.avoid: Do not treat embolisation as definitive without the follow-up scan. In the 59-patient cohort, 20 of 59 patients (34%) ultimately required surgery despite embolisation, and one patient died three months after the procedure. Half the embolisations in the systematic review (95 of 196 tumours, 48.5%) were for non-bleeding lesions, so the 45% surgery-avoidance figure mixes acute and elective indications and should not be quoted as the post-rupture figure. Surgery avoided is also a process endpoint and the pooled median follow-up was 31 months — too short to find malignant transformation in a lesion that was never removed.
standard.note: The interval before re-imaging is not defined by any study. A contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 to 12 weeks, once the haematoma has resolved enough to see the lesion, is the common practice and is a convention.

alt.t: Send the embolised or resected lesion, and any later specimen, for subtyping — a bled adenoma in an obese woman is where sonic hedgehog adenoma hides.
alt.pref: Any patient who presents with symptomatic bleeding, particularly an obese woman or a drinker. Sonic hedgehog adenoma was the only subgroup associated with symptomatic bleeding in the 533-adenoma series — 71% versus 14% in every other subgroup — and its 22 of 533 cases (4%) had all previously been counted as unclassified. In the 261-patient multivariate bleeding model the ranking was sonic hedgehog subtype odds ratio 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52), regular alcohol consumption 9.16 (2.47-34.01), beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 (1.78-23.55) and diameter 1.02 per millimetre (1.01-1.03); body-mass index was not associated with bleeding at all (P=0.71), which is worth knowing before attributing a bleed to obesity. Bleeding in that cohort occurred in adenomas below 5 cm, including in 2 of the 4 pregnant women. Prostaglandin D synthase is the specific immunohistochemical marker for sonic hedgehog adenoma, but it is insensitive and was assessed in only 5 cases.
alt.avoid: Do not report argininosuccinate synthase 1 as a bleeding-risk score. It was proposed as a marker of adenomas at high risk of haemorrhage; on reanalysis across 408 adenomas its overexpression marks the sonic hedgehog subgroup as part of a periportal expression programme (correlation with GLI1 expression R=0.75, P<0.0001), and ASS1 messenger RNA expression was not associated with any specific clinical feature in 390 adenomas.
alt.note: Knowing the subtype after a bleed changes the surveillance of the rest of the liver and the counselling about a future pregnancy. It does not retrospectively change the acute management. Read the predictors with their limits: 97% of the 261-patient cohort was operated, bleeding status was ascertained at or before resection so the model predicts prevalent rather than future bleeding, and the two dominant predictors are a subtype that needs sequencing and an exposure that is modifiable — neither of which the 5 cm rule touches. The 5 biopsy-related bleeds excluded from that cohort are the one harm attributable to the diagnostic pathway itself, and a decision model would need them back.

alt.t: Where the bleeding lesion is exophytic, peripheral and small and the patient is stable in a centre without interventional radiology, a limited resection is a reasonable alternative to transfer.
alt.pref: A peripherally placed segment II-III or segment VI exophytic lesion, where a non-anatomical resection is quick and the transfer is long. There is no comparative evidence for this at all; it is an availability argument.
alt.avoid: Do not generalise this to a central or large lesion, and do not use it to justify a major hepatectomy in an unstable patient when transfer for embolisation is achievable. The positional bleeding figures the earlier draft of this page cited in support could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn, which leaves this option resting on surgical convenience rather than on evidence.

avoid.t: Do not embolise a pregnant patient before 24 weeks if a peripheral resection will do.
avoid.pref: EASL: prior to 24 weeks, surgery may be preferred, especially for smaller resections located at the periphery of the liver, because the ionising radiation exposure and intravenous contrast agents associated with transarterial embolisation may be harmful to the fetus. Obstetric and fetal-medicine input belongs in the decision.
avoid.avoid: In an exsanguinating patient this reverses: control the bleeding by whichever route is fastest. The rule applies to the planned or semi-urgent case, not to the resuscitation.

avoid.t: Do not treat a haemorrhage as proof that the lesion was benign.
avoid.pref: Exclude malignancy once stable, as EASL requires, and review any specimen with expert liver pathology.
avoid.avoid: Bleeding and transformation are not mutually exclusive. In the 533-adenoma series histological haemorrhage was present in 52% of tumours and symptomatic bleeding in 14% of patients, while male sex carried an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2) and CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation 9.3 (4.4-20.0) for malignant transformation — so the same lesion can do both, and a man who has bled is at the top of both lists. The adenomas that bleed are large, and the adenomas that transform are large, so the two associations are confounded in every series.

gates.name: 6 · Pregnancy, and the woman planning one
crit: Pregnant, or planning a pregnancy, with a known or suspected adenoma
Adenoma under 5 cm, not exophytic and not growing
Adenoma 5 cm or larger, or any lesion that has grown
A previous pregnancy complicated by the adenoma
The diagnosis has not been confirmed on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent
gates.ask: Can this woman go ahead, and how closely do I have to watch her?

standard.t: Confirm the diagnosis on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent before you counsel her, because a quarter of these lesions are not adenomas.
standard.pref: Every woman of childbearing age with a suspected adenoma, ideally before pregnancy. In the multicentre prospective cohort, 18 of 66 women (27%) with a suspected adenoma under 5 cm on conventional imaging were shown on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI to have focal nodular hyperplasia instead — a lesion with no haemorrhage risk, no malignant potential and no follow-up requirement. The authors' own conclusion was that the misdiagnosis rate justifies the scan simply to prevent unnecessary anxiety.
standard.avoid: Do not counsel on the strength of an ultrasound or a non-hepatobiliary MRI, and do not perform the confirmatory scan during pregnancy if it can be done before or after — in that study the postpartum scan was used where a definitive diagnosis was lacking at inclusion. The national resection audit found the same error at the other end of the pathway: focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected lesions under 50 mm, and absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI independently predicted a change of diagnosis (adjusted odds ratio 1.8).
standard.note: This is the one place on the page with prospective multicentre data, and the finding is about diagnosis rather than treatment. Grade B refers to the misclassification rate, not to any management question. Note that the 27% figure also means this cohort is cleaner than routine practice and therefore not representative of it — the women enrolled had all had their diagnosis confirmed on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI, which most surveilled women have not.

standard.t: An adenoma under 5 cm is not a reason to discourage pregnancy, and is not by itself a reason for caesarean section.
standard.pref: The woman with a hepatobiliary-contrast-confirmed adenoma under 5 cm that is not exophytic and not growing. In 48 such women followed through 51 pregnancies with protocolised ultrasound, growth occurred in 13 of 51 pregnancies (25.5%) with a median increase of 14 mm; no rupture or haemorrhage occurred in any of the 51 pregnancies, and the one lesion that grew beyond 7 cm was embolised.
