ACG 2024: pregnancy is not generally contraindicated in adenoma under 5 cm (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). EASL: in the presence of adenomas under 5 cm that are not exophytic or growing in size, there is no data supporting elective caesarean and vaginal delivery can be pursued. The Italian multisociety guideline sets the pregnancy surveillance schedule at ultrasound at 14, 20, 26, 32 and 38 weeks and at 6-12 weeks postpartum, graded very low quality (D), conditional.
standard.avoid: Forty-eight women is the entire prospective evidence base, every lesion in it was under 5 cm, and the study can say nothing about the 5 cm-and-larger lesion — which is exactly where practice diverges most. Zero ruptures in 51 pregnancies has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7%, so the data license pregnancy in a small adenoma without establishing that the residual risk is negligible. A quarter of pregnancies showed growth, so minimal risk is not the same as no change, and growth was measured by ultrasound while the diagnosis was made by MRI, so the growth figures come from the less reproducible modality. There are no subtype data, so the quarter that grew cannot be characterised and the subtypes that bleed below 5 cm are not identified.
standard.note: The earlier 12-woman, 17-pregnancy retrospective series reached the same conclusion from weaker data: 4 adenomas grew, one woman had caesarean sections at 36 and 34 weeks for an assumed rupture risk after her largest lesion grew from 32 to 75 mm, one had radiofrequency ablation in the first trimester, and all 17 pregnancies ended well with no rupture. Read its selection: the institutional policy was to treat adenomas of 5 cm or more that did not regress before pregnancy, so the women who reached pregnancy had already been filtered as low-risk, two had been operated and one embolised beforehand, and the same single patient generated two of the three caesareans. Zero events in 17 pregnancies has an upper 95% bound of roughly 20%. The historical comparator those authors cite — 44% maternal and 38% fetal mortality — comes from published case reports of women presenting acutely, the most biased possible control.

standard.t: Monitor with ultrasound every 6 to 12 weeks through pregnancy and into the early puerperium, with obstetric liaison written into the plan.
standard.pref: Every pregnant woman with an adenoma, whatever its size. EASL: adenoma in a pregnant woman requires close follow-up using frequent ultrasound every 6 to 12 weeks to monitor size, and liaising with the obstetric team is essential if the lesion increases in size. The prospective cohort monitored growth with ultrasound throughout pregnancy specifically so that intervention remained possible, and that is what happened in the one patient who needed it.
standard.avoid: Do not stop watching at delivery. In the combined cohort and systematic review of 11 local patients plus 90 patients with 99 pregnancies, 15 adenoma-related haemorrhages occurred: 8 during pregnancy, 2 during labour and 5 postpartum. Maternal death occurred in 5 of those 15 and fetal death in 5 of 15 — but that is the case fatality of the published haemorrhage literature, in which only catastrophic events reach print, and it cannot be used to estimate the consequence of haemorrhage in an unselected pregnancy. The puerperal events are the reason surveillance runs past the birth.
standard.note: The interval is EASL's, and no study has compared intervals. Ultrasound is the modality because it is repeatable without contrast or ionising radiation; a lesion that becomes hard to see on ultrasound needs a non-contrast MRI rather than a CT.

opts.name: Resect before conception
opts.when: EASL: in women with large tumours, or in whom adenoma had complicated previous pregnancies, surgical resection may be recommended.
opts.pref: The woman with a lesion comfortably over 5 cm, or an exophytic lesion, or a previous pregnancy complicated by the adenoma, who has time before she wants to conceive and in whom the resection is not major. It removes the question rather than managing it.
opts.avoid: Do not impose a major hepatectomy on a young woman whose lesion is still falling on risk-factor modification. Pregnancy should also not be delayed indefinitely for a resection that keeps being deferred — name the date.

opts.name: Embolise before conception, or during pregnancy if it grows
opts.when: EASL: for growing lesions, embolisation can be considered; prior to 24 weeks surgery may be preferred because ionising radiation and intravenous contrast may be harmful to the fetus.
opts.pref: A large central lesion for which resection would be major, and the growing lesion in the second half of pregnancy — which is what happened in the single intervention in the prospective cohort, at 26 weeks for a lesion that had passed 70 mm. Multicentre data show the median diameter falling from 76 to 48 mm by a median 5.5 months.
opts.avoid: Major complications in 6 of 59 patients (10%) in the non-pregnant multicentre series, symptoms unchanged at 3 months (P=0.134), and viable tissue left behind that EASL would then have you resect if it persists. Before 24 weeks, prefer a peripheral resection where one is feasible.

opts.name: Proceed with close surveillance
opts.when: Not a guideline position for a lesion over 5 cm; EASL's size-based advice is drawn at 5 cm and its pregnancy advice below it.
opts.pref: The woman with a 5 to 6 cm, non-exophytic, non-beta-catenin lesion who wants to conceive now and accepts 6-weekly ultrasound. Of 73 pregnancies in which the adenoma was untreated, 39 (53.4%) remained stable, 11 (15.1%) regressed and 23 (31.5%) grew. All 15 adenoma-related haemorrhages in that pooled literature occurred in lesions of 6.5 cm or larger and none below that size.
opts.avoid: The 6.5 cm figure is the smallest size among published haemorrhages, not a derived threshold — it is governed by what gets written up, and a case report of a small adenoma bleeding in pregnancy is far less likely to be published than a dramatic large one. ACG 2024 nonetheless adopts 6.5 cm as a treatment trigger, so a publication-limited minimum has become a criterion in a GRADE guideline. The pooling is itself a problem: a modern institutional cohort is combined with decades of case reports across incompatible eras of imaging and obstetric care, the stability figures use a denominator of 73 against 99 pregnancies reviewed so a quarter lack trajectory data, growth is undefined, and there are no subtype data anywhere — so the paper cannot say whether the bleeding lesions were sonic hedgehog or beta-catenin exon 7/8, the obvious alternative explanation to size. Fatal rupture during pregnancy is reported: one of the six haemorrhages in the 40-patient adenomatosis natural-history cohort was fatal and occurred during pregnancy. Do not present no reported bleed below 6.5 cm as a safe threshold.

alt.order: Ordered as EASL orders them for a lesion over 5 cm, and the order carries no comparative evidence: no cohort, let alone a trial, compares pre-conception treatment with surveillance in an adenoma over 5 cm. This is among the most commonly asked questions in the disease and one of the least well answered. The prospective cohort was restricted by design to lesions under 5 cm, so the evidence stops precisely where the question starts; expert practice has already diverged from the written guideline more generally, with 79% of responding European experts declining routine resection of an adenoma over 5 cm after lifestyle change and only 51% having the multidisciplinary team the guideline assumes.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item: the programme's position on a 5 to 7 cm adenoma in a woman who wants to conceive now. EASL recommends treating a large lesion; the Dutch prospective data stop at 5 cm and report zero ruptures in 51 pregnancies, which has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7%; and all 15 haemorrhages in the pooled literature occurred at 6.5 cm or above — a smallest published size rather than a derived threshold, now adopted as a treatment trigger by ACG 2024. Whatever is chosen, it should be written down before the next such patient is in clinic, and it should name who counsels her — hepatology, hepatobiliary surgery, interventional radiology and obstetrics together. Registry: diameter, subtype, intervention or none, growth during pregnancy, mode of delivery, haemorrhage, maternal and fetal outcome.

avoid.t: Do not use CT for surveillance in pregnancy.
avoid.pref: Ultrasound for the interval monitoring, and non-contrast MRI if the lesion cannot be followed sonographically.
avoid.avoid: EASL's reason for preferring surgery to embolisation before 24 weeks is the ionising radiation and intravenous contrast; the same reasoning applies to a surveillance CT, where there is no urgency to justify it. A CT is still the right test in suspected rupture.

avoid.t: Do not discourage a pregnancy on an unconfirmed diagnosis.
avoid.pref: Get the hepatobiliary-contrast MRI first; 27% of these referrals turned out to be focal nodular hyperplasia, which carries no restriction at all.
avoid.avoid: Advising against pregnancy, or recommending a hepatectomy, on the basis of a lesion that has not been characterised is the most consequential avoidable error on this page. Expert practice in this disease has already diverged from the written guideline — 48 of 61 responding European experts (79%) advise against routine resection of an adenoma over 5 cm after lifestyle change, and only 31 of 61 (51%) have the benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary team the guideline assumes — which makes a confident unilateral answer in clinic hard to defend.

gates.name: 7 · Multiple adenomas and adenomatosis
crit: More than one adenoma on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI
Ten or more adenomas
Bilobar distribution that no single resection can clear
A germline HNF1A mutation, MODY3 diabetes, or a family history of liver adenoma
A male patient, glycogen storage disease, or microadenomas on a previous specimen
gates.ask: Does the number change what I do, or do I still manage this by the largest lesion?

standard.t: Manage by the size and behaviour of the largest lesion, not by the count.
standard.pref: Every patient with multiple adenomas. EASL: the management of patients with multiple adenomas should be based on the size of the largest tumour (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2), because the clinical presentation and risk of bleeding and malignant transformation do not differ from patients with a single adenoma. In a 122-patient surgical series the risk of complications was not related to the number of adenomas but to size over 5 cm, and especially to the telangiectatic (inflammatory) and unclassified subtypes; steatotic adenomas had a low complication risk. In the 533-adenoma molecular series the rate of haemorrhage or malignant transformation was the same whatever the number of adenomas.
standard.avoid: Do not read manage by the largest as the others do not matter. In the long-term adenomatosis cohort, 87% of patients had subtype-homogeneous nodules, so sampling one nodule generally characterises the others — but the 13% who do not are the reason a single biopsy cannot be treated as a survey of the liver, and that figure comes from the nodules that happened to be sampled, which were not randomly chosen.
standard.note: A single nodule on imaging was itself associated with malignant transformation in the 533-adenoma series (odds ratio 4.1, 95% CI 1.7-11.7), which is the opposite of the intuition that more lesions mean more danger. Read the long-term adenomatosis data the same way: malignant transformation occurred in 1 of 40 patients (2.5%) over a median 10.6 years, and haemorrhage in 6 of 40 (15%) of whom 5 bled as the presenting event — so surveillance at any threshold would not have prevented most of them. With 40 patients those rates rest on one and six events respectively.

standard.t: Resect the dominant lesions where the disease is unilobar or where the largest can be cleared — and do not try to clear the liver.
standard.pref: Unilobar disease, or widespread disease with one or two lesions that have crossed the size or growth threshold. EASL: hepatic resection might be considered in unilobular disease, and in those cases with more widespread adenoma, resection of the largest adenomas may be an option (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2). In the 40-patient adenomatosis natural-history cohort, 37 (93%) had surgery at diagnosis and 4 (10%) needed repeat resections over a median 10.6 years of follow-up.
standard.avoid: EASL records that microscopic adenomatous foci escaping radiological detection have been found in resected livers with widespread bilobar disease, so no resection short of hepatectomy makes the liver adenoma-free and none should be presented to the patient that way. Expect to come back: in the 40-patient adenomatosis cohort 4 patients (10%) needed repeat resections over a median 10.6 years.
standard.note: A 134-patient surgical series reports 8.1% morbidity and no mortality for resection in this disease, without a Clavien-Dindo distribution; repeat resection in a previously operated liver is not that operation. Count on the first operation being the easiest one. And note what the long-term cohort cannot tell you: 37 of 40 patients (93%) had surgery at diagnosis, so its complication rates describe treated disease, and resected nodules leave the risk set without any competing-risk accounting. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Look for a germline HNF1A mutation and offer genetic counselling where the picture fits.
standard.pref: A young patient with many adenomas, a family history of liver adenoma, or early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes. In the 40-patient long-term adenomatosis cohort, 6 patients (15%) carried germline HNF1A mutations and all 6 of the familial cases did. In the founding genotype-phenotype series, 7 of 44 HNF1A-mutated adenomas (16%) carried one germline and one somatic mutation, and those germline carriers were younger (23 versus 40 years, P=0.0001), had larger tumours (142 versus 69 mm, P=0.02), more nodules (P=0.04) and less oral contraceptive use (P=0.002) — a different disease wearing the same name.
standard.avoid: Do not restrict the search to women, and do not assume small nodules in this setting are safe. In familial HNF1A adenomatosis the disease occurs equally in men and women with the higher bleeding rate in the men, and in the long-term cohort two male patients with familial adenomatosis bled from nodules measuring only 20 mm and 40 mm — among the clearest documented haemorrhages far below the 5 cm line anywhere in this literature, and an argument for subtype and sex rather than for relocating the threshold downwards.
standard.note: Familial adenomatosis is associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3, so a fasting glucose and a three-generation family history for diabetes and liver tumours belong in the first clinic visit, and metabolic genetics belongs at the board.

alt.t: Where the number is large but every lesion is small, surveillance is defensible.
alt.pref: Many small HNF1A-inactivated or inflammatory lesions in a woman, with risk factors being modified and the dominant lesion well under 5 cm. Over a median 10.6 years in the 40-patient cohort, malignant transformation occurred in 1 patient (2.5%) and haemorrhage in 6 (15%), 5 of those at the time of diagnosis; 87% of patients had subtype-homogeneous nodules, so one biopsy generally characterises the liver.
alt.avoid: That cohort was 93% operated at diagnosis, so its complication rates describe treated disease and cannot be read as the natural history of observation, and with 40 patients the 2.5% and 15% rest on one and six events with confidence intervals compatible with most published figures. Set the 2.5% ten-year transformation rate against what the radical alternative costs: in the European registry series of 49 transplants for adenomatosis there were three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure.
alt.note: The pooled contemporary surveillance figures — 88.5% stable or regressed, 0.5% symptomatic bleeding, 0.8% malignant transformation across 699 patients — include multiple-lesion patients but do not report them separately.

alt.t: Transarterial embolisation of the dominant lesions is a reasonable way to reduce burden without taking parenchyma.
alt.pref: Bilobar disease where a resection clearing the dominant lesions would be major, and the patient who has already had one resection. In 59 patients the median diameter fell from 76 to 48 mm by a median 5.5 months (P<0.001), and in the 851-patient systematic review elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%).
alt.avoid: Major complications in 6 of 59 (10%) with one death three months after the procedure, 20 of 59 (34%) still requiring surgery, no symptom improvement at 3 months (P=0.134), and viable tissue left behind in a liver that already has lesions you are not treating. EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates, so using it here is a departure that should be recorded as one.

avoid.t: Do not list a patient for transplantation on lesion number.
avoid.pref: Use the transplant gate's named routes, every one of which requires something beyond the count.
avoid.avoid: EASL: liver transplantation is not recommended in multiple adenoma, but might be considered in individuals with underlying liver disease (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2). The 122-patient series drew the conclusion explicitly — because complications were unrelated to the number of adenomas, patients with multiple adenomas do not need liver transplantation. The local hepatic adenoma protocol says the same thing in its own words: lesion number alone does not qualify, and more than 10 lesions is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

avoid.t: Do not use the old ten-lesion definition of adenomatosis as though it were a risk category.
avoid.pref: Record the count, the dominant diameter, the distribution and the subtype, and let the dominant lesion drive management.
avoid.avoid: EASL replaced the term liver adenomatosis with multiple hepatocellular adenomas precisely because precise counting of adenomas by imaging can be challenging and because risk is driven by the size of the largest nodule. The local transplant protocol nevertheless uses more than 10 lesions as one necessary condition of its adenomatosis route — that is a policy threshold inherited from the registry literature, not a risk threshold, and it should be described as one in any narrative that invokes it.

gates.name: 8 · Syndromic and vascular settings
crit: Glycogen storage disease type I, III or IV
Abernethy malformation or another congenital portosystemic shunt
Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis or another vascular liver disease
Beta-thalassaemia, haemochromatosis or another iron-overload state
McCune-Albright syndrome, or a paediatric or adolescent presentation
gates.ask: Is there an underlying disease here that I should be treating instead of, or before, the adenoma?

standard.t: In glycogen storage disease, treat metabolic control as the first-line adenoma therapy and keep lifelong imaging surveillance.
standard.pref: Every patient with glycogen storage disease type I, III or IV. EASL: in glycogen storage diseases the lifelong risk of adenoma is particularly high, the tumours frequently appear in the second or third decade, nearly half are inflammatory adenomas, and no HNF1A-inactivated adenoma has been observed in this setting; reduction in size and/or number has been observed following optimal metabolic control. The 533-adenoma molecular series confirms both halves of that. The ACMG practice guideline for glycogen storage disease type I puts numbers to the burden: 70-80% of patients over the age of 25 have at least one hepatic adenoma, progression defined as growth or increase in number occurs in about 50%, and the mean age at adenoma presentation is 14.8 years — so these are decisions made in children and adolescents. Chromosome 6p gain or 6q loss is present in about 60% of GSD Ia adenomas.
standard.avoid: Do not import the general adenoma surveillance interval or the general resection threshold, and do not expect a serum marker to help: the ACMG guideline states that alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen do not predict malignant transformation and cannot be used for surveillance, which leaves imaging size as the only monitored variable and reimports the 5 cm convention into a population in which it was never tested and in which adenomas are multiple from adolescence. EASL's own interval here is annual ultrasound from 0 to 10 years and biannual beyond 10 years; the GSD type I surveillance table uses liver ultrasound every 12 to 24 months to age 16 and then CT, ultrasound or contrast MRI every 6 to 12 months from age 16, earlier in those who already have adenomas. And weigh the operation differently: 53.1% of the 99 published liver transplants for hepatic adenoma were in glycogen storage disease patients, and metabolic decompensation, renal disease and the neutropenia of type Ib change the operative calculus entirely.
standard.note: Get metabolic genetics into the room. The local hepatic adenoma protocol requires it for glycogen storage disease cases and requires glycogen storage disease therapy to be optimised and renal, metabolic and systemic manifestations assessed before transplantation is considered. Note the status of the guidance you are following: the ACMG document states explicitly that its recommendations are considered expert opinion, applies no recommendation grading to its adenoma sections, gives the 50% progression figure without a time base, and predates both the sonic hedgehog subtype and the exon-specific beta-catenin gradient — so a near-universal complication of a rare disease is being managed by convention borrowed from cohorts of young women on oral contraceptives.

standard.t: In a congenital portosystemic shunt, define the anatomy and ask whether the shunt can be closed before you touch the nodule.
standard.pref: Any patient, and especially any child, with Abernethy malformation or another congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Nodules in this setting span focal nodular hyperplasia, adenoma and carcinoma, and resection can impede a future shunt occlusion procedure — which is the argument for defining the vascular anatomy first. The local hepatic adenoma protocol requires exactly this: define the Abernethy anatomy and assess whether shunt closure or another vascular intervention is feasible before transplantation.
standard.avoid: The evidence that shunt closure shrinks the nodule is one paediatric case report, and it does not show regression: an HNF1A-inactivated adenoma fell from 11.5 cm to 10 cm four months after closure, a 13% change in diameter that does not meet the RECIST threshold for response and sits within the range of between-scan measurement variability, in a lesion that remained far above any size at which management would change. Do not present shunt closure as an established adenoma treatment; present it as the intervention that addresses the cause, to be assessed by a service that performs them. And do not assume the nodule is benign — carcinoma occurs in this setting, and adenomas arising in vascular liver disease are reported to behave atypically with higher transformation risk.
standard.note: Ruling out a congenital portosystemic shunt in a child with a liver tumour is itself a reason to look at the portal vein deliberately rather than incidentally; a hypoplastic portal vein is present in most cases. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: In vascular liver disease, raise your suspicion of beta-catenin activation and of carcinoma, and biopsy the nodule with a full immunohistochemical profile.
standard.pref: Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis, obliterative portal venopathy and other vascular liver disease. Patients with liver vascular disease developed beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas significantly more often in the 411-patient series (P=0.04), and fibrosis in the non-tumour liver was itself associated with malignant transformation (odds ratio 3.8, 95% CI 1.1-11.4). Imaging follow-up protocols for these patients should be designed to identify an adenoma early and distinguish it from a large regenerative nodule, and every biopsied hepatocellular lesion should get the full immunohistochemical panel.
standard.avoid: Do not try to separate adenoma from a large regenerative nodule and from carcinoma on imaging alone in a Budd-Chiari liver — the three overlap and the stakes differ completely. And read the evidence honestly: this rests on a single subgroup P value of 0.04 in a cross-sectional series, plus case reports. It is a reason to biopsy and to look harder, not a quantified risk.
standard.note: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is explicitly outside EASL's benign-tumour guideline and is covered separately in the non-cirrhotic portal hypertension literature; do not manage it from this page.

alt.t: Record the rarer associations, but do not invent management rules for them.
alt.pref: Iron overload from beta-thalassaemia or haemochromatosis, McCune-Albright syndrome, familial adenoma with maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3, and endogenous androgen excess states such as polycystic ovary syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome. EASL lists these as rarer associations with implications for management, and recording them is how a cluster is eventually recognised.
alt.avoid: There is no subtype, surveillance or threshold data for any of them beyond case reports. Manage the adenoma by sex, size, growth and subtype, and manage the association on its own terms.
alt.note: In an unusual association, the registry entry is the deliverable. Nothing will be learned about these settings from single cases that are not recorded.

alt.t: A paediatric or adolescent presentation belongs with the metabolic and vascular services from the first visit, not after the adenoma workup fails.
alt.pref: Adenoma under 18. The underlying diagnosis is far more likely to be glycogen storage disease, a congenital portosystemic shunt or germline HNF1A disease than sporadic hormone-related adenoma: the mean age at adenoma presentation in glycogen storage disease type I is 14.8 years, the published congenital portosystemic shunt case was a 9-year-old, and in the long-term adenomatosis cohort all 6 familial cases carried germline HNF1A mutations with germline carriers presenting at a median 23 years against 40 for the rest.
alt.avoid: Do not apply adult hormone-withdrawal and 5 cm logic to a child. None of the threshold data include children, and in glycogen storage disease the lesions appear in the second or third decade against a background that is itself the problem.

avoid.t: Do not resect a glycogen storage disease adenoma before the metabolic team has had a run at it, unless the lesion itself forces your hand.
avoid.pref: Size, growth or suspected transformation still force the operation. Short of that, optimise control and reimage, because reduction in size and number following optimal metabolic control is a reported phenomenon in this specific setting.
avoid.avoid: The regression claim rests on case series within a rare disease and is not a treatment effect established against a comparator. It justifies a trial of control before an operation in a stable patient; it does not justify deferring an operation in a growing or atypical lesion.

avoid.t: Do not assume an adenoma in a syndromic patient behaves like a sporadic one.
avoid.pref: Record the syndrome, expect the subtype distribution to differ, and set the surveillance interval from the syndrome rather than from the adenoma.
avoid.avoid: The subtype distribution genuinely differs: never HNF1A-inactivated in glycogenosis, enriched for inflammatory there, enriched for beta-catenin exon 3 in vascular liver disease, and in familial HNF1A adenomatosis equally distributed between the sexes with the higher bleeding rate in men. Every one of those breaks an assumption the sporadic pathway is built on.

gates.name: 9 · Suspected malignant transformation
crit: Male patient, or a confirmed CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation
Growth despite adequate risk-factor modification, or a lesion of 8 cm or more
Cellular atypia, pseudoglandular formation, cholestasis, nuclear beta-catenin or strong diffuse glutamine synthetase on biopsy
A TERT promoter mutation, where sequencing has been done
A borderline lesion, or a hepatocellular neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential, on pathology review
gates.ask: Is there carcinoma in this lesion already, and how would I actually know?

standard.t: Accept that transformation is usually diagnosed on the specimen rather than on surveillance imaging, and let that shape the decision to resect.
standard.pref: Any high-risk lesion. In the 218-patient series, 25 patients had malignant transformation; the median diameter of the transformed adenomas was 10 cm, only 3 of the 25 were 5 cm or smaller, and all three of those arose in a liver with fibrosis or iron overload. In the male pathology series, malignant transformation occurred in 4 of 27 adenomas (14.8%), in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions. The pooled figure across 1,635 adenomas is 68 transformations (4.2%), with only 3 of those 68 (4.4%) in a tumour under 5 cm and the smallest transformed adenoma in the literature measuring 4 cm. The practical consequence is that imaging surveillance of a high-risk lesion is not a transformation-detection strategy; resection is.
standard.avoid: Do not offer surveillance as a way of catching transformation early in a beta-catenin-activated adenoma or in a man. And do not read the size association in reverse. In the 533-adenoma molecular series the 50 mm cut-off did not significantly separate malignant transformation (13.1% versus 7.6%, P=0.053), so a small high-risk lesion is not safe merely for being small. The '4.4% below 5 cm' statistic is a proportion of the numerator and not a risk, and it is partly an artefact of how few sub-5 cm adenomas entered the pooled denominator at all; the review it comes from carries three mutually inconsistent denominators (1,635 in the abstract, 1,617 in the table and 1,568 in the discussion), pools case reports with series, and its authors conclude that the 5 cm treatment recommendation is open for debate and that over 95% of patients resected above it are unnecessarily exposed to a procedure with reported morbidity up to 27% and mortality up to 3%. The Taiwanese series contributes the clearest counter-examples: 2 of its 6 malignant transformations occurred in adenomas of 3.5 cm and 4.4 cm, both beta-catenin-activated.
standard.note: Beware the confounding that makes the threshold look validated. In the 164-patient contemporary cohort all six patients who developed carcinoma had lesions of 5 cm or larger — but every one of those six was also beta-catenin-activated or inflammatory, so size and subtype are completely confounded in six events and the paper cannot separate them. The same pattern recurs: in the 134-patient surgical series all four transformations were both beta-catenin-activated and over 5 cm, and in the 218-patient series beta-catenin activation was present in 16 of 25 transformed adenomas. Transformation is also ascertained on the resection specimen, so a lesion resected for being large is more likely to have a small malignant focus found — verification bias working in the same direction as the size association being tested.

standard.t: Rank the risk with the factors that actually predict transformation, and write them in the note.
standard.pref: Every patient in whom transformation is being weighed. From the 533-adenoma series, in order of effect size: TERT promoter mutation odds ratio 67.6 (95% CI 8.3-3072), male sex 18.9 (8.5-44.2), CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation with or without inflammation 9.3 (4.4-20.0), high alcohol intake 4.85, a single nodule on imaging 4.1 (1.7-11.7), fibrosis in the non-tumour liver 3.8 (1.1-11.4), and type 2 diabetes 3.7. TERT promoter mutation was found in 7 of 16 adenomas with malignant transformation (44%) against 179 of 305 carcinomas (59%), 5 of 20 cirrhotic premalignant macronodules (25%) and 0 of 60 typical adenomas; all 7 of the transformed adenomas carrying it also carried a CTNNB1 mutation, which places TERT as a second hit after beta-catenin activation and makes transformation a two-step process.
standard.avoid: These are odds ratios from a cross-sectional surgical series with very wide confidence intervals — the TERT interval runs from 8.3 to 3072, which reflects near-complete separation in a handful of events — and the outcome is a borderline or malignant histological finding at the time of resection, not a prospectively observed event. They rank risk; they do not quantify it, and none has been validated prospectively. TERT promoter mutation is also present by definition only once transformation has occurred, so it confirms rather than pre-empts: it was found in 0 of 60 typical adenomas, a denominator whose upper 95% bound is about 5%, and in 1 of 213 adenomas in a separate series against 3 of 17 borderline lesions. TERT is not always present in adenoma-derived carcinoma either, so a negative result excludes nothing.
standard.note: Beta-catenin activity is not one thing. Exon 3 deletions and substitutions within the D32-S37 beta-TrCP binding site are highly activating and go with strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase and with malignancy; T41 is moderate; S45, K335 and N387 are weak activators in benign tumours. Ask for the codon, not just the exon.

standard.t: Where transformation is confirmed, re-stage completely and re-route the case — and do not assume the standardised HCC transplant pathway is available.
standard.pref: The local hepatic adenoma protocol §3 governs this. Complete multiphasic liver imaging, chest CT and alpha-fetoprotein, state the transformation date and the prior adenoma route in the narrative, and route the case. A candidate with an at-risk background — cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B — is assessed against the standardised HCC pathway on its own terms, and this is the HCC pathway from here. A candidate without an at-risk background, which the protocol calls the usual case, cannot be: OPTN Class 5 imaging classification and LI-RADS are defined for patients at risk for carcinoma, most adenoma-derived carcinoma arises in a non-cirrhotic non-at-risk liver, and the lesion therefore cannot be classified on imaging alone. That candidate needs a non-standard review-board request supported by histologic confirmation, complete staging, tumour burden relative to Milan criteria, alpha-fetoprotein, and an explicit statement of why imaging-based classification does not apply.
standard.avoid: Do not let a normal alpha-fetoprotein reassure you — the protocol states that alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude carcinoma when normal. Extrahepatic metastasis or macrovascular invasion excludes the candidate from the adenoma protocol either way, in both the at-risk and the non-at-risk case.
standard.note: The protocol marks this routing VERIFY against the live Policy 9.5 posting before the first such submission, and that verification has not been performed for this page. Treat the routing as the protocol's reasoning, not as confirmed current policy.

alt.t: Where a borderline lesion is reported, get a second expert liver pathology opinion and sequencing before you call it either thing.
alt.pref: Any report of a borderline hepatocellular lesion, a hepatocellular neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential, or atypical adenoma. 7% of the 533 nodules in the molecular series shared intermediate histological features with carcinoma. In the Dutch nationwide male series the diagnosis changed after expert revision plus sequencing in 33 of 66 cases (50%), with final diagnoses of 20 adenoma, 26 uncertain malignant potential and 20 carcinoma, and the revised category tracked tumour-related mortality (5.6%, 35.7% and 44.4%, P=0.031).
alt.avoid: Do not treat borderline as a diagnosis that permits observation. It is a statement that the specimen cannot be classified, which in a male patient or a beta-catenin-activated lesion should be managed as carcinoma until proven otherwise. The two expert pathology series that have examined this both conclude that the adenoma-versus-well-differentiated-carcinoma distinction is prognostically decisive and frequently got wrong.
alt.note: The dilemmas of atypical and borderline lesions, and the question of which nomenclature to use, are unsettled in the pathology literature itself: the expert reviews concede that the threshold for sufficient versus insufficient atypia remains arbitrary and that the specificity of atypical features in predicting transformation remains to be demonstrated, and the review of the WHO 6th-edition classification adds that in children, patients over 60 and vascular liver disease the morphomolecular features become less well defined, overlap with focal nodular hyperplasia and the line defining malignancy blurs. Name one liver pathologist as the programme's reference reader so that the nomenclature is at least internally consistent.

alt.t: Perform comprehensive specimen or explant mapping in every case and feed the result back to the board.
alt.pref: Every resection and every explant. The local hepatic adenoma protocol §8 specifies the dataset: lesion count, largest size, subtype, CTNNB1 findings, haemorrhage, necrosis, atypia, and occult carcinoma; if malignant transformation is found, stage the explant and define post-transplant surveillance at the transplant-oncology conference.
alt.avoid: Do not accept a specimen report that gives a diagnosis without the subtype and the lesion map. Malignant transformation in 4 of 27 male adenomas, and reclassification of half of all presumed male adenomas on expert review, are numbers that only exist because someone looked for them systematically.
alt.note: This is also the only way the programme will ever know how often its own preoperative assessment was wrong, which is the metric the honest section says matters most.

avoid.t: Do not ablate or embolise a lesion in which transformation is the question.
avoid.pref: Resect it, or biopsy it and then resect it. Both modalities leave viable tissue and neither produces a specimen; EASL already makes residual viable lesion after embolisation an indication for resection.
avoid.avoid: The systematic review of embolisation reported malignant transformation as one of its outcomes of interest precisely because the question cannot be closed by an intervention that leaves the lesion in situ. Treating a possibly malignant lesion with an ablative modality converts a diagnostic problem into an unanswerable one.

avoid.t: Do not use imaging follow-up alone as the surveillance strategy for a beta-catenin-activated adenoma.
avoid.pref: EASL's position is resection irrespective of size in any instance of proven beta-catenin mutation (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2), and the review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size. The molecular support in small lesions is thin but points the same way: among women with adenomas under 5 cm, an at-risk molecular profile identified malignant transformation in 2 of 14 (14%) against 1 of 101 (1%) without it (P=0.007), and no HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman transformed.
avoid.avoid: Read the strength of that honestly: 2 transformations among 14 women is a hypothesis-generating subgroup, not a validated rule, and it is the only evidence offered anywhere for abandoning the size threshold in small lesions. The WHO-review statement is expert assertion with no cited cohort quantifying it. What is firm is the negative: no imaging protocol has been shown to detect transformation in an adenoma early, EASL itself says that identification of beta-catenin-activated adenoma and its distinction from carcinoma is not possible by any imaging technique, and alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude it. Surveillance of this subtype is surveillance for growth, not for transformation, and should be described to the patient as such.

gates.name: 10 · Transplant — the non-standard review-board route
crit: A qualifying guidance route named explicitly in the narrative: syndromic, molecular, adenomatosis, or progressive and complicated
Unresectable after expert hepatobiliary surgical review, with embolisation and ablation exhausted, infeasible or contraindicated
At least 6 months of adequate risk-factor modification documented for non-urgent oestrogen- or weight-associated disease
Multidisciplinary confirmation that non-transplant options are unsafe, infeasible or inadequate and that expected benefit justifies lifelong immunosuppression and graft use
No extrahepatic metastasis and no macrovascular invasion where transformation is confirmed
gates.ask: Has every non-transplant option actually been tried or ruled out, and which guidance route am I naming?

standard.t: Hepatocellular adenoma is not a standardised MELD exception — this is a non-standard review-board request at a recommended MMaT-3, and nothing about it is automatic.
standard.pref: The local UTHealth Houston hepatic adenoma liver transplant protocol V3, policy review 21 September 2026, is the authority for this gate and the page defers to it entirely. Its classification note is specific: the OPTN Board action of 9 June 2025, with guidance effective 1 July 2025, added recommended exception scores for non-standard transplant-oncology diagnoses but did not move hepatocellular adenoma into the standardised list in Policy 9.5.A to 9.5.I. Standard care remains risk-factor modification, observation, resection, embolisation or ablation, and transplantation requires multidisciplinary confirmation that those are unsafe, infeasible or inadequate.
standard.avoid: Do not describe the score as guaranteed or standardised. The protocol notes that secondary literature stating hepatocellular adenoma has been moved into the standardised list is imprecise on that point, and requires re-verification against the live posting before committee adoption and before each submission. Extensions run on a roughly 90-day cycle under Policy 9.4.C with updated imaging, continued unresectability and continued transplant need; the automatic extension provision that applies to HCC candidates at a policy-assigned score does not extend to non-standard transplant-oncology requests. The protocol marks the cycle length and governing subsection VERIFY, and that verification has not been done here.
standard.note: For context when a patient asks why thresholds differ between countries: EASL's position is only that transplantation is not recommended in multiple adenoma but might be considered in individuals with underlying liver disease (evidence level III, grade of recommendation 2), and the UK NHSBT Liver Advisory Group Fair Transplant Working Group published national guidance in 2025 assigning patients with benign liver tumours to four eligibility categories (A, B1, B2 and C). That guidance is a consensus document with no underlying cohort, it does not define how adenoma size, number, subtype or prior intervention map onto the categories in any form that can be audited, it makes no reference to beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog status, and its own working group concedes that categorisation still requires individual case review. Its detailed criteria have not been read into this page and should not be quoted from it. [PROTOCOL]

standard.t: Name the qualifying route in the narrative, and record the CTNNB1 exon and codon where the route is molecular.
standard.pref: The protocol's molecular route requires a documented CTNNB1 activating alteration with the exon and codon recorded. Exon 3 non-S45 alterations carry the strongest association with malignant transformation and satisfy the route directly. S45 exon 3 and exon 7/8 alterations do not by themselves: the selection committee must document an additional risk feature — size, growth, haemorrhage, a syndromic driver, or diagnostic uncertainty about transformation — and record why the expected benefit justifies deceased-donor organ use and lifelong immunosuppression. Where the molecular result is an immunohistochemical surrogate rather than sequencing, the narrative must state which, and its limitations.
standard.avoid: The exon split is an institutional refinement that restricts rather than expands the route, and the protocol requires it to be described as such, because the OPTN guidance itself does not distinguish exon categories. But do not read the split as a statement that S45 is low risk. In 220 adenomas, 373 carcinomas and 17 borderline lesions, S45 was a weak activator in benign tumours yet was identified at similar frequency in mutated adenomas and in mutated carcinomas, and in most carcinomas with a weakly activating mutation a second hit raised activity — duplication of the mutant allele in 60% of those, a second more active CTNNB1 mutation in 33%, or APC inactivation. Chromosome 3p gain or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity was present in 37% of 27 weakly mutated carcinomas against 3% of 75 moderately or highly mutated ones, and in none of 34 adenomas. Those authors concluded that adenomas with S45, and with all high or moderate mutants, should be identified by precise immunohistochemical criteria or by mutation screening — and that S45 gives an intense but heterogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern that is difficult to recognise, so identifying it reliably needs sequencing.
standard.note: This is the clearest live disagreement on the page. The protocol's restriction is defensible as organ stewardship; it is not defensible as a claim about S45 biology. See the honest section and approval item 8.

standard.t: Record the full disease dataset before the request, and keep imaging on the 90-day cycle while listed.
standard.pref: The protocol §6 dataset: adenoma number, dominant and aggregate dimensions, bilobar distribution, growth trajectory, haemorrhage and rupture history, symptoms, prior resections, embolisations and ablations, and pathology and molecular results; full blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, INR, liver tests, and alpha-fetoprotein where transformation remains a concern. While listed, multiphasic MRI or CT every 3 months, aligned with the 90-day exception-extension cycle, shortened for active growth, haemorrhage or suspicion of transformation. Immediate re-review for a new rupture, major haemorrhage, rapid growth, suspected carcinoma, or a newly feasible non-transplant option.
standard.avoid: None of these intervals is a risk threshold derived from outcome data; the 3-month interval exists because the extension cycle is 90 days. Do not present it to the patient as a biologically determined surveillance schedule. And the trigger that most often gets missed is the last one: a newly feasible non-transplant option is a reason to come off the pathway.
standard.note: Post-transplant, for adenoma without malignant transformation the protocol mandates standard transplant clinical and graft surveillance with no routine tumour imaging; where occult or known transformation is found, risk-adapted surveillance with chest and abdominal cross-sectional imaging every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years and then 6-monthly through year 5, individualised to stage and pathology. Syndrome-specific follow-up continues for glycogen storage disease and for shunt manifestations that transplantation does not fully correct.

opts.name: Syndromic route
opts.when: Adenoma in the presence of glycogen storage disease or Abernethy malformation / congenital portosystemic shunt. The protocol requires the narrative to explain separately why transplantation is medically necessary.
opts.pref: The patient in whom the underlying disease rather than the adenoma is driving the need, and in whom shunt closure or metabolic optimisation has been assessed and found insufficient. Glycogen storage disease accounted for 53.1% of the 99 published cases in the systematic review and for 16 of the 49 European registry transplants for adenomatosis.
opts.avoid: A syndrome is not an indication. Metabolic genetics for glycogen storage disease and vascular expertise for Abernethy malformation are required at the table, and feasibility of shunt closure must be assessed first.

opts.name: Molecular route
opts.when: Unresectable adenoma with a documented CTNNB1 activating alteration, with the exon and codon recorded.
opts.pref: An unresectable exon 3 non-S45 lesion, which satisfies the route directly on the strength of an odds ratio of 9.3 (95% CI 4.4-20.0) for malignant transformation and the highly activating mutant classification.
opts.avoid: Not available on an S45 or exon 7/8 result alone — those need a documented additional risk feature and a recorded justification. And not available on an immunohistochemical surrogate presented as sequencing; state which was done.

opts.name: Adenomatosis route
opts.when: Unresectable liver adenomatosis with more than 10 adenomas AND at least one of: recurrent or life-threatening haemorrhage or prior rupture not controllable by embolisation or targeted resection; confirmed or strongly suspected malignant transformation, or a high-risk molecular subtype; a syndromic driver or underlying liver disease independently threatening hepatic function; or documented progression despite at least 6 months of adequate risk-factor modification with liver-directed options exhausted or contraindicated.
opts.pref: The patient with recurrent uncontrollable bleeding, or with transformation, in a liver that resection cannot clear. The route is deliberately conjunctive and the protocol requires dominant lesion size, growth trajectory, complication history and molecular status to be recorded.
opts.avoid: Lesion number alone does not qualify. The European registry experience is the cautionary case: of 49 transplants performed for adenomatosis, true malignant transformation was present in only 17 explants (35%), there were three operative deaths and five retransplantations, and three patients developed carcinoma recurrence, all fatal — so roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively. The same series found that 15 of 64 cases coded as adenomatosis in the registry were not adenomatosis at all once verified, which is a warning about every registry-based figure in this disease.

opts.name: Progressive or complicated route
opts.when: All three of: unresectable after expert hepatobiliary surgical review; unresponsive to appropriate non-operative management, such as observation after stopping oestrogen-containing medications, efforts to maintain an ideal body weight, transarterial embolisation or thermal ablation; and progressive or complicated by haemorrhage, rupture or malignant transformation, with lesion size documented.
opts.pref: The patient who has genuinely exhausted the liver-directed options. The protocol allows that an unsafe or clearly futile intervention need not be performed solely to demonstrate failure, provided the reason is documented — which is the clause that keeps this route honest rather than performative.
opts.avoid: Do not invoke it before embolisation and ablation have been assessed by the services that perform them, with the assessment in writing. Elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%) in one systematic review and reduced median diameter from 76 to 48 mm in a 59-patient multicentre series, so exhausted has to mean assessed and rejected, not untried — but present the other half too, because the patient will ask: 34% of embolised patients still needed surgery, 10% had a grade D complication, one died at three months, and symptoms were unchanged.

alt.order: Ordered as the local protocol lists them, not by outcome — no comparison of routes exists, and the whole indication rests on 142 US transplants across 33 years and 49 European ones across 27. Published survival is good: patient survival 94.2%, 89.7% and 86.3% at 1, 3 and 5 years over a median 62.9 months in the UNOS cohort of 142, with graft survival 89.3%, 84.1% and 80.0%, and 95% at all three points across 99 published cases. Read those as what a heavily selected cohort achieves rather than as a treatment effect, and read the other side of them: crude waitlist mortality was 9.0% among the 199 listed, death occurred in 26 of 142 (18.3%) during follow-up, 24 of the 142 transplants were for adenoma diagnosed only incidentally on the explant, 89.4% had no carcinoma at all, and the median laboratory MELD at transplant was 8 at a median age of 34.5 — young people with preserved liver function, so almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than the disease. The registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, and the 99 published cases report 6.0% mortality against the registry's 18.3%, a threefold disagreement the authors attribute to publication bias in their own review.
alt.flagnote: Three ratification items. First: does the programme open an adenoma transplant route at all, and under whose governance? The indication is rare enough that most centres will see one candidate in several years, graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and neither supporting dataset has a comparison group managed without transplantation — so the claim of excellent outcomes in well-selected patients is unfalsifiable from these data. Second: does the S45 and exon 7/8 restriction stand as written, given that the genotype-phenotype data make S45 a special case — a weak activator in benign tumours that is duplicated to high activity in most carcinomas, with chromosome 3p gain or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity in 37% of weakly mutated carcinomas against none of 34 adenomas — rather than a low-risk one? Third: who verifies the live OPTN Policy 9.4 and 9.5 text and the current transplant-oncology guidance before each submission, and on what cycle? Several items in the protocol are marked VERIFY and remain unverified. One further caution from the full-text read: 15 of 64 cases coded as adenomatosis in the European registry were not adenomatosis once verified, and the US analysis rests on the same kind of coding plus a free-text search with no case-level verification, so every registry figure behind this gate should be read as provisional. Registry: route named, full lesion dataset, CTNNB1 result and method, review-board decision, waitlist events, donor source, explant pathology concordance with the preoperative diagnosis, perioperative morbidity and mortality, graft and patient survival, and malignant transformation.

alt.t: Treat living donation and donor-source ethics review as part of this conversation, not an afterthought.
alt.pref: A young patient with benign disease and a willing related donor is exactly the scenario in which living donation is raised. The protocol requires deceased- or living-donor transplantation to comply with current OPTN allocation requirements and institutional donor-source ethics review.
alt.avoid: Do not let the availability of a living donor substitute for the selection decision. The question of whether this patient should be transplanted at all is answered before the question of where the graft comes from, and the registry outcomes that make this indication look safe come overwhelmingly from deceased-donor transplantation.
alt.note: No tumour-specific immunosuppression regimen is established for benign adenoma, and the protocol directs standard institutional operative and immunosuppression protocols.

avoid.t: Do not list a patient whose disease is safely resectable with an adequate remnant.
avoid.pref: Resect. This is a named exclusion in the local protocol and it is the commonest reason an adenoma case should not reach the review board.
avoid.avoid: EASL does not recommend transplantation in multiple adenoma, and the 122-patient surgical series concluded explicitly that because complications were unrelated to lesion number, patients with multiple adenomas do not need liver transplantation.

avoid.t: Do not list a stable low-risk adenoma that is responding to hormone withdrawal or weight intervention.
avoid.pref: Keep modifying the risk factors and keep imaging. The protocol names this as an exclusion unless another explicit guidance route is independently met and transplantation is separately justified.
avoid.avoid: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm fell below 5 cm at a median 104 weeks with no documented complication, and 69% shrank after oral contraceptives were stopped. A patient on that trajectory is not a transplant candidate, and listing resets nothing about the underlying driver.

avoid.t: Do not transplant on a suspicion of carcinoma that a biopsy could have settled.
avoid.pref: Where histology is obtainable, obtain it. The protocol's non-standard malignant-transformation route requires histologic confirmation precisely because imaging cannot classify these lesions in a non-at-risk liver.
avoid.avoid: In the European registry series, true malignant transformation was present in only 17 of 49 explants (35%) from patients transplanted for adenomatosis, despite suspected or proven carcinoma being the dominant indication; the authors' own conclusion was that the decision should rely on morphological data and histological evidence of malignant transformation. A substantial fraction of those grafts went to patients whose explant did not confirm the indication.

quickref.title: HCA molecular subtypes — frequency, marker, and what each changes
quickref.intro: The eight-subgroup classification of 533 adenomas from 411 patients across 28 centres — a resection series, so every frequency below is a frequency among operated adenomas. This is the table that forks the pathway.
rows: HNF1A-inactivated (H-HCA) — 33.5%

LFABP lost in tumour hepatocytes. Marked steatosis; diffuse homogeneous signal dropout on opposed-phase T1, MRI sensitivity 87-91% and specificity 89-100%. Lowest histological haemorrhage rate of any subgroup (39%). No malignant transformation in any H-HCA under 5 cm in a woman (0 of 47). Germline mutation in 8%, with adenomatosis and MODY3 diabetes. Never seen in glycogen storage disease.
Inflammatory (I-HCA) — 34%

SAA and CRP positive, LFABP retained. IL6ST 77%, FRK 9%, STAT3 4%, GNAS 3%, JAK1 1%, non-mutated 6%. Obesity, alcohol, high oestrogen exposure; raised CRP, GGT and alkaline phosphatase; least often symptomatic at presentation (30%, P<0.0001). Strong T2 signal and persistent delayed enhancement, sensitivity 85-88% and specificity 88-100% with extracellular agents, falling to 80.9% and 77.3% with gadoxetic acid. Enriched in glycogen storage disease.
Beta-catenin exon 3 (b-ex3) — 7%

Nuclear beta-catenin, strong diffuse glutamine synthetase. Cell atypia, pseudoglandular formation, cholestasis. Male, androgen exposure, younger than other subgroups, enriched in vascular liver disease (P=0.04). The highest malignant risk: odds ratio 9.3 (95% CI 4.4-20.0) for transformation. No imaging phenotype. And the marker is unreliable: only 27% of 33 mutated adenomas tested showed the textbook strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern, and sequencing in a 66-patient male series found 4 mutated adenomas that immunohistochemistry and expert review had both missed.
Beta-catenin exon 3 plus inflammatory (b-ex3 I-HCA) — 6%
Both phenotypes; counted with b-ex3 as at-risk. About half of all beta-catenin-activated adenomas are also inflammatory, so an inflammatory phenotype does not exclude the high-risk driver.
Beta-catenin exon 7/8, with or without inflammation — 4% plus 4%

Faint patchy glutamine synthetase, no nuclear beta-catenin. Not associated with increased malignant risk, but a bleeding subtype: odds ratio 6.47 (95% CI 1.78-23.55) for haemorrhage in the 261-patient multivariate model, against 1.02 per millimetre for diameter. Mutually exclusive with exon 3 mutations and with HNF1A.
Sonic hedgehog (shHCA) — 4%

Focal INHBE deletion producing an INHBE-GLI1 fusion. Described in 2017 and absent from EASL 2016; previously counted as unclassified. 100% female, higher BMI. The dominant bleeding subtype: symptomatic bleeding 71% versus 14%, P<0.0001, and odds ratio 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52) in the 261-patient multivariate model — twenty times the per-centimetre size effect. No reliable routine immunohistochemical marker exists: prostaglandin D synthase is specific but insensitive and was assessed in 5 cases, argininosuccinate synthase 1 is sensitive and not specific and is not associated with haemorrhage, and molecular profiling remains the reference. So the single most actionable bleeding predictor in this disease cannot be measured where the 5 cm decision is made.
Unclassified (U-HCA) — 7.5%

No specific morphology, immunophenotype or imaging feature, and no identified driver. Counted as not at risk on that basis alone, which is weaker ground than it sounds: in the male pathology series, malignant transformation occurred in unclassified as well as beta-catenin-inflammatory adenomas, and unclassified was the second commonest subtype there at 25.9% — two to three times the rate in series using full molecular analysis, which suggests incomplete characterisation rather than a distinct biology. Proteomics reduces the unclassified fraction from about 7% to under 2%.
WHO 6th edition, as described in a 2026 review

Five subtypes rather than eight: H-HCA 30-35%, inflammatory 35-40%, beta-catenin-activated 10%, beta-catenin-activated inflammatory 10-15%, sonic hedgehog 5-10%, with under 5% unclassified when full immunohistochemistry and molecular testing are applied. Quoted complication rates are bleeding 10-20% and malignant transformation 4-8%. Management positions stated: beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas are resected or ablated whatever their size, and sonic hedgehog adenomas carry a high haemorrhage risk even below 5 cm. Read as a narrative review, not as the classification: it cites no cohort quantifying either management statement, its frequencies come from the same French and Korean series that generated the classification, its complication rates are resection-series figures presented without that caveat, and its own subtype percentages differ from the same authors' 2022 review without explanation.
Korea, low contraceptive use (121 patients, 138 adenomas)

A different disease in a different population: 38.8% male, only 5.0% with oral contraceptive exposure, inflammatory 38.4% and beta-catenin-activated 26.1% — roughly four times the European beta-catenin proportion — with carcinoma present in 16.7% of the beta-catenin-activated adenomas. An imaging score predicted beta-catenin subtype with AUROC 0.92 on derivation and 0.91 on an internal split, not external validation; applied to a European case mix with a quarter the beta-catenin prevalence its positive predictive value would fall sharply. The study was supported by Bayer Korea, which markets the hepatobiliary contrast agent its score relies on, and hepatocellular adenoma was not suspected at all in 31.6% of the original radiology reports — a finding the score's claimed accuracy is not reconciled with. The Taiwanese series points the same way: 58% male, 75% inflammatory, only 3 women with any contraceptive exposure.
quickref.foot: At-risk versus not-at-risk, as the authors defined it: at-risk is beta-catenin exon 3 with or without inflammation, plus sonic hedgehog; not-at-risk is everything else. The stratification matters most where the size rule is weakest: among women with adenomas under 5 cm, an at-risk profile identified malignant transformation in 2 of 14 (14%) against 1 of 101 (1%) without it (P=0.007), and no HNF1A-inactivated adenoma under 5 cm in a woman transformed (0 of 47). Both figures rest on very few events — two transformations and a zero numerator — so this is a hypothesis-generating subgroup and not a validated rule, and it is nevertheless the only evidence offered anywhere for replacing the size threshold in small lesions. Immunohistochemistry with four antibodies (SAA, LFABP, glutamine synthetase, beta-catenin) reproduced the major subtypes with sensitivity and specificity 0.85-0.93 in that series, but sequencing in a separate 66-patient male series found 4 beta-catenin adenomas that immunohistochemistry and expert review had both missed, and only 27% of mutated adenomas show the glutamine synthetase pattern the algorithms key on. Subtype accuracy does not deteriorate in small lesions: 80% versus 87.5% for imaging below and above 5 cm (P=0.45), 75% versus 84.6% for biopsy with immunohistochemistry (P=0.48). Within one patient, 87% of multiple adenomas share a subgroup, so one biopsy generally characterises the liver. Beta-catenin activity is graded, not binary: exon 3 deletions and D32-S37 substitutions are highly activating, T41 moderate, and S45, K335 and N387 weak in benign tumours — but in carcinomas carrying a weak mutation a second hit usually raises activity, so ask for the codon and do not read a weak mutation as a weak lesion.

quickref.title: The 5 cm convention — what the supporting series actually show, and what the direct tests found
quickref.intro: For the conversation about whether this particular lesion has earned an operation. Read top to bottom: the first block is where the number came from, the second is what happened when the threshold hypothesis was tested directly, and the third is what happens to adenomas that are watched.
rows: Where 5 cm comes from

Not a trial, and not a derivation. EASL 2016 calls it the accepted clinically relevant size cut off and supports its central premise — that in nearly all cases of spontaneous rupture or haemorrhage the lesion is at least 5 cm — with a single citation, grading the recommendation at evidence level II-3 with recommendation strength 2, its weaker category. Behind it sit three surgical datasets: a systematic review of 28 articles and 1,176 patients, a 5-centre series of 124, and a pooled review of 1,635 adenomas
Haemorrhage, systematic review (n=1,176)

315 of 1,160 patients (27.2%) but only 118 of 748 lesions (15.8%) — the two denominators differ by nearly twofold, and a rule derived per lesion and applied per patient is not the same rule. Rupture 114 of 651 (17.5%). Haemorrhage was the first symptom in 126 of 184 bleeding cases (68.5%), so most bleeding is unpreventable by surveillance at any threshold. 91.2% of the pooled patients had been resected, and the authors label their own figures maximum risks for that reason
Haemorrhage, 5-centre series (n=124)

Rupture in 31 (25%). The size dichotomy that actually predicted rupture was fitted at 7 cm, not 5 cm: odds ratio 7.78 (95% CI 2.22-26.32), an interval compatible with effects an order of magnitude apart. Recent hormone use independently predicted rupture at 4.46 (1.49-13.33). Malignancy in 5 (4%), smallest malignant adenoma 8 cm. The authors then recommended resecting above 4 cm — three different numbers in one paper, and the one that entered the guidelines has the least statistical support. Patients with very small adenomas were explicitly excluded, so no tumour under 5 cm ruptured describes the sampling frame
Malignant transformation, pooled (n=1,635)

68 transformations (4.2%) overall; 50 of 1,617 (3.1%) in series; 4.5% of the 1,462 resected. Only 3 of the 68 (4.4%) in a tumour under 5 cm, smallest 4 cm. That 4.4% is a proportion of the numerator, not a risk. The paper carries three mutually inconsistent denominators (1,635, 1,617 and 1,568), pools case reports with series, and its own authors conclude the 5 cm treatment recommendation is open for debate and that over 95% of patients resected above it are unnecessarily exposed to a procedure with reported morbidity up to 27% and mortality up to 3%
Direct test 1 — is there a threshold? (n=261, full subtyping)

No. Diameter was modelled continuously and was an independent risk factor for bleeding at odds ratio 1.02 per millimetre (95% CI 1.01-1.03, P<0.001), roughly a 1.2-fold increase in odds per centimetre, and the authors state plainly that they did not identify a threshold size. The predictors that dominate are sonic hedgehog subtype 21.02 (5.05-87.52), regular alcohol 9.16 (2.47-34.01) and beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 (1.78-23.55); body-mass index was not associated (P=0.71). Bleeding occurred below 5 cm, including in 2 of the 4 pregnant women. 97% of the cohort was operated, and bleeding status was ascertained at or before resection, so the model predicts prevalent rather than future bleeding
Direct test 2 — where does a cut-point fall if you look for one? (n=195 lesions)

At 35 mm, 15 mm below the convention: bleeding in 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above (53%, P<0.001). But the institution's own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected and therefore sectioned, bleeding grades I to III were pooled so trivial intratumoral blood counts alongside peritoneal rupture, no beta-catenin-activated adenoma was identified in the whole series and 48% were unclassifiable — so it cannot exclude subtype as the real driver, and 35 mm is a best fit in one dataset, not a validated threshold
Direct test 3 — what does 50 mm separate? (n=533)

Histological haemorrhage, yes: 65% above versus 40% below, P<0.0001. Symptomatic bleeding, no: P=0.29 — and symptomatic bleeding is the outcome the operation is meant to prevent. Malignant transformation did not reach significance either: 13.1% versus 7.6%, P=0.053. Histological haemorrhage was present in 52% of tumours against symptomatic bleeding in 14% of patients, so the two are dissociated
Why the apparent size gradient is partly arithmetic (n=122 patients, 365 adenomas)

Microscopic haemorrhage 0.9%, 19% and 68% and macroscopic 0%, 5% and 24% across the under-2 cm, 2-5 cm and over-5 cm strata; malignancy 0, 1 (2%) and 9 (9%). The gradient is largely a property of the denominator: this was a resect-everything policy, the sub-2 cm stratum consists almost entirely of incidental microadenomas found inside specimens removed for a different and larger lesion, and the over-5 cm stratum consists of the lesions that prompted the operation — two non-comparable populations. Counting 365 lesions in 122 patients inflates the small-lesion denominator mechanically, and microscopic haemorrhage found only because the specimen was sectioned cannot occur in a lesion left in situ. The one malignancy under 5 cm was in a man taking steroids
Documented events below 5 cm

Haemorrhage down to 1 cm in the pooled literature, and in 6 of the 13 size-reporting articles in the systematic review. Bleeding from nodules of 20 mm and 40 mm in two men with familial adenomatosis. Malignant transformation at 3.5 cm and 4.4 cm in the Taiwanese series, both beta-catenin-activated, and at 4 cm as the smallest in the pooled review. In every one of those counter-examples a high-risk subtype, male sex or androgen exposure was present — which argues for subtype and sex rather than for relocating the threshold downwards
The most favourable modern dataset (n=187-193)

Haemorrhage in 13% of patients with a lesion of 5 cm or more against 0% below. But on 10 events, at a median bleeding size of 8.7 cm, and a zero rate in roughly a hundred patients has an upper 95% bound of about 3% — so the data are compatible with a modest rather than an absent risk below 5 cm, and support a cut-point well above 5 cm as readily as 5 cm itself. 69% of patients regressed after oral contraceptive cessation
Time to regression below 5 cm (n=194)

Only 8.5-15.3% at 26 weeks — the exact point at which EASL and ACG advise resection — rising to 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks and 69 of 118 (58.5%) eventually at a median 104 weeks (95% CI 80-128). Strongly size-dependent: median 63 weeks under 7 cm, 109 weeks at 7-10 cm, 208 weeks over 10 cm (P<0.001). No complication occurred anywhere in that follow-up. So the six-month decision point captures roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually cross the line
Contemporary surveillance (n=699, 7 studies)

88.5% stable or regressed (95% CI 74.9-95.2); symptomatic bleeding 0.5% (0.1-3.5); malignant transformation 0.8% (0.4-1.9); median follow-up 2 to 5.8 years. One to two orders of magnitude below the historical references the rule was built on (bleeding 20-40%, transformation 4-10%). Read with its flaw: in five of the seven studies lesions were pulled out of the surveillance group by intervention as soon as they grew, so these are the outcomes of the lesions allowed to remain under observation. Six of seven carried moderate to serious risk of bias, four different definitions of size change were used, and removing one study moved pooled progression from 11.5% to 18.1%
Contemporary surveillance-dominant cohort (n=164)

76.2% managed by surveillance; rupture 1.8%; regression 18.4%; no malignant transformation at all among those watched. In the 4-5 cm band, 26.8% of the cohort, 22.7% regressed — about 11 of 44 patients. All six patients who developed carcinoma had lesions of 5 cm or more, but every one was also beta-catenin-activated or inflammatory, so size and subtype are completely confounded in six events
What it costs to act on the threshold (n=222 resections)

44 of 222 Dutch resections for presumed adenoma (20%) were performed on lesions under 50 mm — outside the size indication the guidelines give. The postoperative diagnosis differed from the preoperative one in 43% overall, 70% of lesions under 50 mm and 78% of male patients, and focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected sub-50 mm lesions. Independent predictors of a changed diagnosis: lesion under 50 mm adjusted odds ratio 3.4, male sex 3.7, absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI 1.8
How the threshold is graded, and whether anyone follows it

The Italian multisociety guideline is the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework, and it grades every size-based recommendation — the 5 cm resection trigger, the resect-all-men rule, the 6-month decision point and the whole surveillance schedule — as very low quality of evidence (D), strength 2, conditional. The French consensus grades every adenoma recommendation C1, C2 or D2, its weakest categories. In a European expert survey, 48 of 61 respondents (79%) advise against routine resection of an adenoma over 5 cm after lifestyle change, and only 31 of 61 (51%) have the multidisciplinary team the guideline assumes; the response rate was 21%. One institution in the published literature used 4 cm, then 5 cm, then a subtype-and-sex rule across a single study period, each adopted without new local data, with comparable outcomes under all three
quickref.foot: Read the two halves together, and state the conclusion plainly rather than leaving it implied: 5 cm is a convention. It was not derived, the three studies usually cited for it fit cut-points at 7 cm, 35 mm and nowhere, the guideline that fixed it in place calls it accepted and grades it II-3 with conditional strength, and the only guideline to appraise it formally grades it very low quality. That does not make it wrong, and this page keeps the recommendation: the alternative — subtype-directed management — requires tissue and sequencing that EASL declines to recommend routinely, and the subtype that best predicts bleeding cannot be identified on imaging at all. What the evidence does not support is describing 5 cm to a patient, or in a note, as a risk threshold. The rupture and malignancy series are surgical cohorts whose rates describe patients selected for operation; the surveillance series are their mirror image, describing lesions already judged safe to watch. EASL's growth trigger is a 20% diameter increase taken from RECIST 1.1, a framework built for response assessment in solid malignancy and never validated in a benign liver lesion; on a 5 cm lesion it is 1 cm, small enough that the measurement convention in the radiology report decides whether the trigger fires.
