quickref.title: The transplant routes — what the local protocol requires
quickref.intro: Hepatocellular adenoma is a non-standard review-board request, not a standardised exception. These are protocol conditions, not evidence thresholds.
rows: Allocation status
Not a standardized diagnosis under OPTN Policy 9.5. Guidance-aligned rare-indication non-standard exception; recommended score MMaT-3; approval and extension are not automatic
Syndromic route
Glycogen storage disease, or Abernethy malformation / congenital portosystemic shunt — and the narrative must still explain why transplantation is medically necessary
Molecular route

Unresectable adenoma with a documented CTNNB1 activating alteration, exon and codon recorded. Exon 3 non-S45 satisfies the route; S45 and exon 7/8 do not alone and need a documented additional risk feature and a recorded justification
Adenomatosis route

Unresectable, more than 10 adenomas, AND one of: uncontrollable or recurrent haemorrhage or prior rupture; confirmed or strongly suspected transformation or a high-risk subtype; a syndromic driver or underlying liver disease threatening hepatic function; or progression despite 6 months of adequate risk-factor modification with liver-directed options exhausted. Number alone does not qualify
Progressive or complicated route

All three of: unresectable after expert hepatobiliary review; unresponsive to appropriate non-operative management; progressive or complicated by haemorrhage, rupture or transformation, with lesion size documented
Prerequisites for every route

Stop oestrogens and anabolic androgens with contraceptive and pregnancy counselling; weight and metabolic management; optimise glycogen storage disease therapy; define Abernethy anatomy and assess shunt closure; document feasibility and outcome of resection, staged resection, embolisation and ablation, with the reason recorded where an intervention would be unsafe or futile. Repeat imaging after about 6 months of risk-factor modification before declaring progression in non-urgent disease
Named exclusions

Safely resectable with an adequate remnant; stable low-risk adenoma responding to hormone withdrawal or weight intervention; no qualifying route; inadequate hepatobiliary surgical or interventional-radiology assessment; uncontrolled infection, prohibitive comorbidity, active uncontrolled substance-use disorder; extrahepatic metastasis or macrovascular invasion where transformation is confirmed
Transformation routing

Re-stage completely and re-route. With an at-risk background, assess against the standardised HCC pathway on its own terms. Without one — the usual case — the standardised pathway is unavailable because OPTN Class 5 and LI-RADS are defined for at-risk livers; submit a non-standard request with histologic confirmation, complete staging, burden relative to Milan criteria, AFP, and an explicit statement of why imaging classification does not apply
Extensions

Roughly 90-day cycle under Policy 9.4.C with updated imaging, intervening treatment or complications, and continued unresectability and transplant need; the automatic extension provision for HCC candidates at a policy-assigned score does not apply
Explant requirement
Comprehensive explant mapping and pathology: lesion count, largest size, subtype, CTNNB1 findings, haemorrhage, necrosis, atypia, and occult carcinoma
What the transplant evidence actually is

Two series and a review, all retrospective and all heavily selected. UNOS 1987-2020: 199 patients listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%); 142 transplanted at a median age 34.5, 79.6% female, 22.5% children, median laboratory MELD at transplant 8 — these were not patients with failing livers; 127 of 142 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with patient survival 94.2%, 89.7% and 86.3% at 1, 3 and 5 years and graft survival 89.3%, 84.1% and 80.0%. Because the recipients were young with preserved liver function, almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than to the disease. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis. The registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. European registry, adenomatosis: 49 transplants with true malignant transformation in 17 explants (35%), three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively; and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases were not adenomatosis at all once verified. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against 18.3% in UNOS, a threefold disagreement the authors attribute to publication bias in their own review
quickref.foot: The exon split is an institutional refinement that restricts rather than expands the molecular route, and the protocol requires it to be described as such, because the OPTN guidance does not distinguish exon categories. It is also the page's sharpest live disagreement: the genotype-phenotype data make S45 a weak activator in benign tumours but found it at similar frequency in mutated adenomas and in mutated carcinomas, with a second hit raising activity in most carcinomas carrying a weak mutation — allele duplication in 60% of those, a second more active mutation in 33%, or APC inactivation — and chromosome 3p gain or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity in 37% of weakly mutated carcinomas against 3% of moderately or highly mutated ones and none of 34 adenomas. Those authors therefore recommended that S45 adenomas be identified rather than reassured about, and noted that S45 gives a glutamine synthetase pattern difficult enough to recognise that sequencing is needed. For the outcome context behind this gate, see the row above: none of it is comparative, none of it records lesion size, and in one series a third of the explants did not confirm the indication. Several items in the protocol are marked VERIFY against the live OPTN posting and remain unverified on this page; it must not be used for a listing decision without that check.

honest.t: This page is a draft, not policy. Hepatocellular adenoma has no ratified Memorial Hermann system roadmap and no companion guideline-alignment worksheet. The only local documents behind it are the hepatic adenoma liver transplant protocol V3, which governs the transplant gate and nothing else, and the Master Workup and Staging CPG, which supplies the front-door workflow and the hepatic adenoma row of its staging matrix. Everything between the front door and the transplant gate is assembled here from EASL 2016 and the literature since.
honest.why: Said first so that nothing further down reads as a settled institutional decision. Where a statement does come from a local document it is attributed to that document by name; where it does not, it is a proposal for the group to ratify or reject. This version has been revised after a full-text read of all 46 papers in the depot, which changed numbers, grades and in several places the direction of a claim — the changes are set out in the provenance note.

honest.t: 5 cm is a convention, not a derived threshold — and the page now says so in the gate rather than only here.
honest.why: This is the single most important thing the full-text read established, and it is graded D for that reason. EASL 2016 describes the number in its own words as the accepted clinically relevant size cut off, supports its central factual premise with one citation, and grades the recommendation at evidence level II-3 with recommendation strength 2, its weaker category. The Italian multisociety guideline, the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework with PICO questions and ROBINS-I appraisal, grades every size-based adenoma recommendation as very low quality of evidence (D) with conditional strength. Where the threshold has been tested directly it has not held. In 261 patients with full molecular subtyping, diameter was modelled continuously and acted as an independent risk factor for bleeding at an odds ratio of only 1.02 per millimetre (95% CI 1.01-1.03, P<0.001), with the authors stating that they did not identify a threshold size; sonic hedgehog subtype carried 21.02, alcohol 9.16 and beta-catenin exon 7/8 6.47 in the same model, so size is the weakest of the significant predictors and the only one the pathway acts on. The one study designed to derive a cut-point derived 35 mm. The series universally cited for the rule fitted its cut-point at 7 cm and its authors recommended resecting above 4 cm. In 533 adenomas the 50 mm line separated histological haemorrhage (P<0.0001) but not symptomatic bleeding (P=0.29), and the malignancy difference did not reach significance (P=0.053). Haemorrhage is documented down to 1 cm and transformation at 3.5 cm. Four fifths of responding European experts decline to follow the rule. The page keeps the recommendation anyway, because the alternative requires sequencing that EASL declines to recommend routinely and because the best bleeding predictor cannot be seen on imaging — but it should never again be described in a note or to a patient as a risk threshold.

honest.t: The strongest-looking size gradient in this literature is an artefact of counting lesions instead of patients.
honest.why: The 122-patient, 365-adenoma French series reports microscopic haemorrhage of 0.9%, 19% and 68% and macroscopic haemorrhage of 0%, 5% and 24% across its under-2 cm, 2-5 cm and over-5 cm strata, with malignancy in 0, 1 and 9 — and it is the origin of both the apparent dose-response for size and the resect-all-men rule. The full-text read shows why the gradient cannot be read as a risk gradient. The series was run under a policy of systematic resection, so the indication for surgery was not size. The sub-2 cm stratum consists almost entirely of incidental microadenomas discovered inside specimens removed for a different and larger lesion, while the over-5 cm stratum consists of the lesions that prompted the operation: the two strata are not comparable populations. Counting 365 lesions in 122 patients inflates the small-lesion denominator mechanically, which drives the small-stratum rates down arithmetically — and the same per-lesion versus per-patient conflation runs through the whole threshold literature, where the pooled systematic review reports haemorrhage in 27.2% of patients but 15.8% of lesions. Microscopic haemorrhage found only because the specimen was removed and sectioned is also an endpoint that cannot occur in a lesion left in situ, so using it to justify resection is circular. And the one malignancy under 5 cm in that series was in a man taking steroids — the group already managed separately — so the paper's own data are consistent with size being irrelevant once sex and androgen exposure are accounted for. There is no multivariable analysis anywhere in it.

honest.t: Reimage at 6 months, but do not call it a failure until 12. The six-month decision point built into the guidelines is mistimed, not merely conservative.
honest.why: Grade C, and a deliberate deviation from EASL's wording, which indicates resection for a nodule still 5 cm or greater at 6 months. The full-text read makes the case stronger than the earlier draft of this page did. In 194 patients with adenomas over 5 cm, regression below 5 cm had occurred in only 8.5-15.3% at 26 weeks — the exact point at which EASL and ACG advise resection — against 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks and 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks (95% CI 80-128), with time to regression strongly size-dependent (median 63 weeks under 7 cm, 109 weeks at 7-10 cm, 208 weeks over 10 cm, P<0.001) and no complication anywhere in that follow-up. Deciding at six months therefore identifies roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually cross the line, which means the timing of the rule drives over-treatment independently of where the threshold sits. The cohort's own authors proposed exactly this change; no guideline has adopted it. Its limits: 47 of 241 patients were excluded for under six months of follow-up, which removes precisely the patients in whom the guideline rule was applied, so the cohort is enriched for clinicians who already declined to follow it; regression is defined as crossing the 5 cm line, so a fall from 12 cm to 6 cm counts as a non-responder; and there are no subtype data, so it cannot say whether the slow regressors are the lesions that should have been resected anyway. One single-institution series reports that no adenoma regressed significantly at six months, but does not define significant regression and did not look beyond six months.

honest.t: Acting on the threshold has a measured cost, and it is paid in operations on lesions that needed nothing.
honest.why: Grade C, from a Dutch nationwide audit of 222 resections performed for a presumed hepatocellular adenoma. 44 of 222 (20%) were for lesions under 50 mm — outside the size indication the guidelines give. The postoperative diagnosis differed from the preoperative one in 43% of all resected cases, rising to 70% of lesions under 50 mm and 78% of male patients, with independent predictors of lesion under 50 mm (adjusted odds ratio 3.4), male sex (3.7) and absence of hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI (1.8); focal nodular hyperplasia was the final diagnosis in 21% of the resected sub-50 mm lesions, a lesion that needs no treatment and no follow-up at all. Read its limits: it measures diagnostic error rather than harm, reporting no morbidity, mortality or quality-of-life outcome, so the price of those 44 operations is quantified only as a wrong label; the 21% figure rests on roughly nine lesions; the 43% presupposes that the final pathology is right, without central re-review; and it is selected on having been resected, so it cannot say how often the diagnosis is wrong in a lesion that was watched — plausibly more often, which would strengthen its own argument. It is nonetheless the only measurement anyone has made of what a size-driven pathway costs, and it belongs in the consent conversation for an operation at 5 cm.

honest.t: Contemporary surveillance outcomes are one to two orders of magnitude below the figures the 5 cm rule was built on — and they describe the lesions that were allowed to stay under observation.
honest.why: Both halves matter. A PROSPERO-registered meta-analysis of 7 retrospective studies and 699 surveilled patients found 88.5% stable or regressed (95% CI 74.9-95.2), symptomatic bleeding 0.5% (0.1-3.5) and malignant transformation 0.8% (0.4-1.9) over median follow-up of 2 to 5.8 years, against the historical references of 20-40% bleeding and 4-10% transformation. The authors explain the gap: the founding cohorts were small surgical series of 6 to 30 cm lesions in which almost nothing was incidental, and early studies did not distinguish histological from symptomatic bleeding. A separate 164-patient contemporary cohort managed 76.2% of patients by surveillance with rupture in 1.8% and no transformation at all among those watched. The flaw is one the meta-analysis names and cannot repair: in five of the seven pooled studies lesions were pulled out of the surveillance group by intervention whenever they grew or looked worrying, so these are the outcomes of the lesions permitted to remain under observation, not of all adenomas over 5 cm — informative censoring that no random-effects model corrects. Six of seven studies carried moderate to serious risk of bias, four different definitions of size change were used, removing one study moved pooled progression from 11.5% to 18.1%, the bleeding interval spans a thirty-five-fold range, and the pooled cohorts overlap substantially with the individual studies cited elsewhere on this page, so this is a re-presentation rather than independent evidence. The 164-patient cohort has the same problem in simpler form: zero transformation in a group selected by clinicians as low-risk is the expected result of successful selection.

honest.t: Every cohort that appears to validate the threshold confounds size with subtype, usually in fewer than ten events.
honest.why: This is why the threshold looks better in the literature than it is. In the 164-patient contemporary cohort all six patients who developed carcinoma had lesions of 5 cm or more — and every one of those six was also beta-catenin-activated or inflammatory. In the 134-patient surgical series all four transformations were both beta-catenin-activated and over 5 cm. In the 218-patient series beta-catenin activation was present in 16 of 25 transformed adenomas, which had a median diameter of 10 cm. In the Taiwanese series all six transformations were beta-catenin-activated, including the two at 3.5 cm and 4.4 cm. No cohort anywhere has enough events to separate the two variables, and transformation is ascertained on the resection specimen, so a lesion resected for being large is more likely to have a small malignant focus found — verification bias that works in the same direction as the association being tested. The practical consequence is that a programme cannot tell from this literature whether it is the centimetres or the driver mutation that matters, and the only way to find out locally is to record both for every resected lesion.

honest.t: The subtype that best predicts bleeding cannot be identified where the 5 cm decision is made.
honest.why: Grade C, and the reason this page cannot simply replace size with subtype. Sonic hedgehog adenoma is the only subgroup independently associated with symptomatic bleeding (71% versus 14%) and carries an odds ratio of 21.02 (95% CI 5.05-87.52) in the multivariate model — twenty times the per-centimetre size effect. It has no described imaging phenotype. Prostaglandin D synthase is specific but insensitive and was assessed in 5 cases; argininosuccinate synthase 1 is sensitive and not specific, sits downstream of the INHBE-GLI1 fusion as part of a periportal expression programme, and is not associated with histological haemorrhage at all, so any pathway citing it as a bleeding-risk marker is citing a claim the reanalysis refutes. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states plainly that a reliable immunohistochemical marker for routine practice is still lacking and molecular profiling remains the gold standard. Beta-catenin is only marginally better placed: EASL says it cannot be identified by any imaging technique, only 27% of mutated adenomas show the strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern the algorithms key on, nuclear beta-catenin is too insensitive for routine use especially on a biopsy, and sequencing in one male series found 4 mutated adenomas that immunohistochemistry and expert re-review had both missed. So the two subtypes that should override size both require sequencing, and EASL states there is no justification for recommending molecular subtyping as routine practice. That is the bind, and approval item 2 is where the group has to choose a side of it.

honest.t: The WHO 6th edition, as reported in a 2026 review, recommends resecting beta-catenin exon 3 adenomas whatever their size — and asserts it without a cohort.
honest.why: Worth recording precisely because it is the clearest published statement of subtype-over-size, and because its evidential status is weak. The source here is a narrative review presenting the WHO 6th-edition classification of hepatocellular neoplasms, not the classification itself, and this page has not read the classification. The review states that beta-catenin-activated adenomas with an exon 3 mutation are resected or ablated whatever their size because of their risk of malignant transformation, and that sonic hedgehog adenomas carry a high risk of hemorrhage, even if they are smaller than 5 cm. Neither statement is accompanied by a cited cohort quantifying it; both are asserted as established practice. The review has no search strategy and no quality appraisal, its subtype frequencies and complication rates (bleeding 10-20%, transformation 4-8%) are inherited from the same French and Korean series that generated the classification so they are not independent corroboration, those rates are resection-series figures presented without that caveat, and its own subtype percentages differ from the same authors' 2022 review without explanation. It also concedes that no reliable routine marker exists for sonic hedgehog adenoma and that nuclear beta-catenin is insensitive — so it recommends a strategy whose prerequisite it says is unavailable. If the group adopts the exon 3 position it is adopting expert opinion, and the note should say so.

honest.t: Subtype may lengthen a surveillance interval but may not by itself shorten the operating list. A reassuring subtype buys time; an unreassuring one does not commit a patient to an operation that size, growth and sex do not already justify.
honest.why: A local safety convention, grade D, built on an asymmetry in the evidence rather than on a rule anyone has published. EASL states there is no justification for recommending histopathology or molecular subtyping as routine clinical practice, and that whether the risk attributed to beta-catenin activation is independent of sex, size and rate of change is presently unknown. Subtyping has become more informative and more reproducible since 2016, which is the argument for revisiting EASL's position rather than for quietly ignoring it.

honest.t: Exophytic position, visible lesional arteries and a left-lateral location may belong in the operative decision alongside diameter — but the effect sizes this page previously quoted for them could not be confirmed.
honest.why: Downgraded from C to D, and the reason is a failure of this page's own first draft rather than of the literature. The earlier version quoted specific effect sizes — 67% of exophytic lesions bleeding against 11% of intrahepatic, 10 of 13 lesions with visible arteries against 32 of 182, and 11 of 32 segment II-III lesions against 31 of 163 — attributed to a prospective imaging cohort of 45 patients and 195 lesions. That paper is retrospective, not prospective, and the full-text abstraction records only its threshold finding: bleeding in 7 of 129 adenomas below 35 mm (5.4%) against 35 of 66 above (53%, P<0.001), with grades I to III pooled, no beta-catenin adenoma identified in 195 lesions, 48% unclassifiable, and the institution's own 5 cm protocol determining which lesions were resected and sectioned. The positional figures have been withdrawn from the page rather than restated. EASL names exophytic protrusion but builds no rule around it, and no guideline has a composite trigger. The proposal therefore stands as a proposal with its supporting numbers currently unverified, and approval item 7 should not be decided until someone reads that paper's positional analysis directly.

honest.t: Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review with sequencing before accepting the diagnosis, and resect it irrespective of size.
honest.why: The resection rule is grade C and concordant with EASL, ACG 2024 and the Italian 2022 guideline — though the Italian one grades it very low quality (D), conditional, like every other size-based recommendation it makes. It is driven by malignant transformation in 47% of men against 4% of women in one 218-patient tertiary series, in which the transformed adenomas had a median diameter of 10 cm and only 3 of 25 were 5 cm or smaller, all three in a liver with fibrosis or iron overload; by an approximately ten-fold male excess in a second French surgical series; and by male sex as the second strongest independent predictor of transformation in the 533-adenoma molecular series at an odds ratio of 18.9 (95% CI 8.5-44.2). A correction to the earlier draft of this page: it attributed 23.8% occult carcinoma to a US male resection series and 15% to the whole male cohort. Those figures are not supported by the full-text read of that paper, which reports malignant transformation in 4 of 27 male adenomas (14.8%), occurring in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified lesions, with androgen receptor staining positive in half of cases and not associated with transformation. The 23.8% figure has been removed wherever it appeared. The review requirement is grade D local reasoning from one nationwide series in which the diagnosis changed in 33 of 66 men (50%) — a registry-based pathology review with no comparator, selected on tissue availability, whose mortality denominators (18, 14 and 9) do not match its final diagnostic groups (20, 26 and 20) — corroborated prospectively by a national resection audit in which 78% of male patients had their diagnosis changed after resection (adjusted odds ratio 3.7).

honest.t: A small, sequenced, confidently HNF1A-inactivated adenoma in a man who is a prohibitive operative candidate may be observed with a documented reason. No guideline supports this, and after the full-text read, no cohort does either.
honest.why: The earlier draft of this page offered one supporting datum: 7 biopsy-diagnosed male adenomas followed for 22 to 160 months without transformation. That finding is not supported by the full-text read of the paper it was attributed to, and it has been removed. What the male literature actually contains is 4 malignant transformations in 27 male adenomas (14.8%), transformation occurring in unclassified as well as beta-catenin-inflammatory lesions, reclassification of half of presumed male adenomas on expert review with 4 beta-catenin mutations found only by sequencing, and a change of diagnosis in 78% of male resections in a national audit. So this option is now offered as a documented exception with no supporting cohort at all, requiring sequencing, a named reason and a board decision — not as an equivalent option. If the group is not prepared to offer something on that basis, it should say so and delete the option.

honest.t: Surveillance imaging is not a malignant-transformation detection strategy in a high-risk adenoma, and patients should be told so.
honest.why: Grade C, and the uncomfortable part of this disease. Transformation is overwhelmingly diagnosed on the resection or explant specimen: in one series the median diameter of adenomas containing carcinoma was 10 cm and only 3 of 25 were 5 cm or smaller. EASL states that distinguishing beta-catenin-activated adenoma from carcinoma is not possible by any imaging technique, and alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude it — the ACMG glycogen storage disease guideline reaches the same conclusion for its own population, that alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen do not predict transformation and cannot be used for surveillance. TERT promoter mutation is the one molecular marker with near-decisive specificity, but it is by definition present only once transformation has occurred (0 of 60 typical adenomas, upper 95% bound about 5%) and is not always present in adenoma-derived carcinoma, so it confirms rather than pre-empts. No imaging surveillance protocol has been shown to detect transformation early in this disease. Set against that, the contemporary surveillance data give pooled malignant transformation of 0.8% (95% CI 0.4-1.9) in watched lesions — so the honest statement to a patient is that surveillance will not catch transformation early, and that the chance of transformation in a lesion selected as safe to watch is low.

honest.t: Treat an S45 exon 3 CTNNB1 result as uncertain rather than low risk.
honest.why: This contradicts the local transplant protocol's molecular route, which groups S45 with the exon 7/8 alterations as not qualifying on their own. The genotype-phenotype data support a different reading: S45 is a weak activator in benign tumours, but appeared at similar frequency in mutated adenomas and in mutated carcinomas (about 20% of each), and in most carcinomas the weak allele was duplicated to produce high beta-catenin activity — so the authors recommended that S45 adenomas be identified. The protocol's restriction is defensible as organ stewardship; it is not defensible as a claim about S45 biology, and the two things should not be conflated in an NLRB narrative. This is the page's clearest internal disagreement and needs a decision.

honest.t: Transarterial embolisation is more dangerous and less definitive than the earlier draft of this page implied.
honest.why: A direct correction. The earlier version stated that no deaths were reported in either the 59-patient cohort or the 151-patient systematic review. The full-text read records that one patient in the 59-patient cohort died three months after embolisation, that Society of Interventional Radiology grade D complications occurred in 6 of 59 (10%), and that 20 of 59 (34%) ultimately required surgery anyway — so embolisation frequently adds a procedure rather than replacing one. Symptoms were unchanged after the procedure (P=0.134) despite median diameter falling from 76 mm to 48 mm at 5.5 months and 45 mm at 27.4 months, which means the benefit rests entirely on a surrogate: it changes the imaging more reliably than it changes the patient. A median post-treatment diameter of 45 mm leaves the typical lesion just below the threshold rather than eliminated, with no histology, re-entering surveillance. Surgery avoided is a process endpoint, the 84% elective figure rests on 49 patients drawn from multiple small series with no common protocol, the 5.3% major-complication rate pools emergency with elective cases so the elective risk is not separately reported, and a pooled median follow-up of 31 months is too short to detect malignant transformation in a lesion that was never removed. Given that 20-40% of resected presumed adenomas prove to be something else, an unknown fraction of those patients were embolised for focal nodular hyperplasia. None of this removes embolisation from the page; all of it belongs in the consent conversation, and approval item 5 should be decided with it in view.

honest.t: Thermal ablation is downgraded to D: the percutaneous route failed two times in three, and neither series provides tissue.
honest.why: In the founding 18-patient, 45-adenoma series, primary technical efficacy was achieved in only 26 of 45 (57.8%), and it depended almost entirely on approach — 79% for open ablation against 31% percutaneously (P=0.013). The percutaneous route is the only one that offers an advantage over surgery, and it failed two times in three. Two major complications occurred in those 18 patients, a rate of roughly 11%, comparable to or worse than contemporary laparoscopic resection; and although 13 of the 18 were treated because they wished to conceive, no pregnancy outcomes are reported, so the study does not establish that ablation achieved the purpose for which it was done. The stereotactic multiprobe series looks far better — 97.4% technical efficacy in 38 adenomas, no major complications, median follow-up 49.6 months — but it is 14 patients at a single highly specialised centre, a zero complication count in 18 sessions has an upper 95% bound of around 15%, both series report per-lesion rather than per-patient efficacy in patients with multiple nodules, and the senior author consults for the manufacturer of the navigation platform the technique depends on. Neither series obtained histology after ablation, so in a disease whose chief danger is a malignant focus, neither the diagnosis nor its exclusion is established. No study compares ablation with resection.

honest.t: Put bariatric referral on the table before a major hepatectomy in an obese patient whose adenoma burden is metabolic.
honest.why: Grade D. The evidence is three patients in one series, in whom body-mass index fell 31-48% after bariatric surgery with complete regression in two, and seven patients in a pooled review of four studies, in whom body-mass index fell from 41 to 28 (P=0.002) and percentage excess weight loss correlated with reduction in lesion number (Spearman 0.78, P=0.04) but not with reduction in lesion size (0.46, P=0.29) — and size is the variable every threshold is built on, so the positive finding does not touch the decision variable. Formal correlation testing on seven patients is one observation away from non-significance, and both reports are published because the outcome was favourable; a series of non-responders would not have been written up. There is no comparator and no adjustment for simultaneous hormone withdrawal. Crucially, the untreated comparator is not zero: 58.5% of adenomas over 5 cm regress below 5 cm with no intervention at all, so any claimed effect of weight loss has to beat that, and none of these studies is designed to. That is a hypothesis with a mechanism, not a result, and it should be offered as a sequencing question rather than as a treatment. The same applies with more force to drug therapy: the 2026 review of emerging medical therapy for adenoma proposes GLP-1 receptor agonists, JAK/STAT inhibitors, a GLI1 antagonist and fenofibrate, and contains no human efficacy or safety data for any of them in this disease.

honest.t: The guidelines are built on European cohorts of young women on oral contraceptives, and the disease is not the same elsewhere.
honest.why: Two nationwide or multicentre Asian series make this concrete. In Korea, 121 patients with 138 adenomas were 38.8% male with only 5.0% having any oral contraceptive exposure, and beta-catenin-activated adenoma accounted for 26.1% — roughly four times the European proportion — with carcinoma present in 16.7% of those. In Taiwan, 58% of 45 patients were male, only 3 women had ever used oral contraceptives, and 75% of adenomas were inflammatory. Both are pathology-confirmed surgical series, so the male predominance may reflect which patients come to operation as much as which develop adenomas, and both are too small to establish rates; the Korean study's imaging score for predicting beta-catenin subtype was derived and validated in the same cohort (AUROC 0.92 and 0.91 on an internal split, not external validation) and the study was supported by the manufacturer of the contrast agent the score relies on. But the direction is a genuine challenge to a pathway whose hormone-withdrawal window, 5 cm threshold and expectation of regression all come from cohorts that were 85 to 99% female. Neither Asian series performed a size-stratified complication analysis, so two cohorts ideally placed to test the threshold in a different epidemiological setting did not test it. The same applies to glycogen storage disease, where adenomas affect 70-80% of adults from a mean presentation age of 14.8 years and are managed by convention borrowed wholesale from the contraceptive cohorts, and where the governing guideline states explicitly that its recommendations are expert opinion.

honest.t: The 6.5 cm pregnancy trigger is the smallest size among published haemorrhages, not a derived threshold — and it is now a criterion in a GRADE guideline.
honest.why: All 15 adenoma-related haemorrhages in the combined cohort and systematic review occurred in lesions of 6.5 cm or larger and none below. That is a minimum observed size in a literature of case reports and small series, governed by what gets written up: a case report of a small adenoma bleeding in pregnancy is far less likely to be published than a dramatic large one. ACG 2024 nonetheless adopts 6.5 cm as the trigger for treating an adenoma in pregnancy, so a publication-limited minimum has become a treatment criterion in a GRADE-based guideline. The reported case fatality — maternal death in 5 of 15 and fetal death in 5 of 15 — is likewise a property of the published haemorrhage literature, where only catastrophic events reach print, and cannot be used to estimate the consequence of haemorrhage in an unselected pregnancy. The pooled series also mixes a modern institutional cohort with decades of case reports across incompatible eras of imaging and obstetric care, reports its stability figures against a denominator of 73 when 99 pregnancies were reviewed, defines growth nowhere, and contains no subtype data — so it cannot say whether the bleeding lesions were sonic hedgehog or beta-catenin exon 7/8, the subtypes known to bleed below 5 cm and the obvious alternative explanation to size. Fatal rupture during pregnancy is nonetheless real: one of the six haemorrhages in the 40-patient adenomatosis cohort was fatal and occurred during pregnancy.

honest.t: The prospective pregnancy data are reassuring and imprecise, and both cohorts were pre-filtered by the rule they are used to relax.
honest.why: Downgraded from B to C. The only prospective cohort followed 48 women through 51 pregnancies with no rupture or haemorrhage — but zero events in 51 pregnancies has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7%, so it licenses pregnancy in a small adenoma without establishing that the residual risk is negligible. Enrolment was restricted by design to lesions under 5 cm, so it cannot address the question that actually arises in clinic, which is whether a woman with a 6 cm adenoma can safely conceive. Growth occurred in 13 of 51 pregnancies (25.5%) with a median increase of 14 mm, measured by ultrasound while the diagnosis was made by MRI, so the growth figures come from the less reproducible modality; there are no subtype data, so the quarter that grew cannot be characterised. The earlier 12-woman series is weaker still and in the same direction: the institutional policy was to treat lesions of 5 cm or more that did not regress before pregnancy, so the women who reached pregnancy had already been filtered as low-risk, two had been operated and one embolised beforehand, zero events in 17 pregnancies has an upper bound of roughly 20%, and the single patient with substantial growth generated two of the three caesareans. The historical comparator those authors cite — 44% maternal and 38% fetal mortality — comes from 26 published case reports of women presenting acutely, the most biased possible control, so the apparent improvement conflates better selection, better imaging and publication bias. The one genuinely robust finding is diagnostic: 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions were focal nodular hyperplasia on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI.

honest.t: The transplant indication rests on two registries, one of which does not record lesion size and the other of which miscoded a quarter of its cases.
honest.why: Grade D, and the governance question behind approval item 10. In UNOS from 1987 to 2020, 199 patients were listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%) and 142 were transplanted at a median age of 34.5 with a median laboratory MELD of 8 — young people with preserved liver function — of whom 127 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death occurred in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with 5-year patient survival 86.3% and graft survival 80.0%. Because the recipients were not in liver failure, almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than the disease. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis, so the exception pathway functions as a discretionary route rather than a rule. And the registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. The European adenomatosis registry found true malignant transformation in only 17 of 49 explants (35%) with three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight dying of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively — and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases proved not to be adenomatosis at all on verification. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against UNOS's 18.3%, a threefold disagreement its own authors attribute to publication bias in their review. Neither dataset has a comparison group managed without transplantation, so the claim of excellent outcomes in well-selected patients is unfalsifiable from these data. The 2025 UK national guidance assigns patients to four eligibility categories by consensus with no cohort behind them and no reference to beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog status.

honest.t: Registry-coded adenoma data should be treated as unreliable until verified case by case.
honest.why: Not a clinical position but a methodological one that bears on every number this page quotes from a registry, including the local protocol's transplant evidence and any future audit. In the European series, 15 of 64 cases coded as liver adenomatosis in the registry proved not to be adenomatosis once the contributing centres verified them — a quarter of entries wrong. The UNOS analysis depends on the same kind of coding plus a free-text search on the fragment aden, with no case-level verification, so its cohort definition is weaker than the one already shown to fail. The same problem appears clinically rather than administratively: half of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert pathology review, 43% of Dutch resections for presumed adenoma had their diagnosis changed, and 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions in a prospective cohort were focal nodular hyperplasia. The implication for this programme's own registry is that the concordance field — preoperative diagnosis against final pathology — is not an audit nicety but the field that makes every other field interpretable.

honest.t: One named owner for the adenoma plan across hepatology, hepatobiliary surgery and radiology, and one benign-liver-tumour multidisciplinary meeting that sees every case including the ones under surveillance.
honest.why: Grade D, operational. EASL requires that the diagnosis, baseline assessment and agreed follow-up plan always involve a specialist benign liver tumour multidisciplinary team, which is a structural requirement rather than an outcome-tested one. The indirect argument is the European practice-variation survey: where guidelines are weak, practice diverges, and a single named owner is how a six-monthly plan survives three years of imaging and two changes of trainee.

honest.t: No minimum annual volume has been set for elective liver resection for benign disease at this centre, and the acceptable complication rate arguably ought to be lower than for malignancy.
honest.why: No comparative data exist for either half of that. The argument is that the patient is typically a young woman, the disease is benign in most cases, and a 134-patient series reports 8.1% morbidity with no mortality — reported without a Clavien-Dindo distribution, so the clinical weight of those complications is unknown. What the full-text read adds is the other side of the ledger: the pooled review that supplies the 4.2% transformation figure calculates that over 95% of patients resected above 5 cm are unnecessarily exposed to a procedure with reported morbidity up to 27% and mortality up to 3%, and the Dutch national audit found that a fifth of resections for presumed adenoma were performed on lesions under 50 mm, 70% of which had their diagnosis changed afterwards and 21% of which proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia. So what counts as an acceptable complication rate for a benign indication is a governance choice, and the denominator it should be judged against includes the operations that should not have happened. Volume-outcome relationships in liver resection are observational.

honest.t: Nothing on this page has been verified against the live OPTN policy posting, and the page must not be used for a listing decision.
honest.why: The local hepatic adenoma protocol itself marks several items VERIFY and requires rechecking the live OPTN policy and guidance immediately before committee adoption, exception submission or extension — specifically the standardised-versus-non-standard classification, the Policy 9.5 Class 5 imaging criteria and available submission routes, and the Policy 9.4 extension cycle and governing subsection. That recheck has not been performed here.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures the clinical question, the imaging modality and whether a hepatobiliary contrast agent was used, lesion count, dominant and aggregate diameter, exophytic protrusion, segment, visible lesional arteries, growth against the previous study, subtype if assigned and by what method, sex, BMI, oestrogen and androgen exposure, alcohol, diabetes, glycogen storage disease or vascular liver disease, pregnancy or pregnancy intention, haemorrhage history, and prior resection, embolisation or ablation. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check whether the lesion has actually been characterised on MRI with a hepatobiliary agent, because a quarter of referred sub-5 cm lesions prove to be focal nodular hyperplasia; an uncharacterised lesion is returned for imaging rather than discussed. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Front door — referrals arrive through the Master Workup and Staging CPG's intake pathway; its hepatic adenoma row sets the minimum staging dataset as liver MRI with hepatobiliary characterisation, haemorrhage and rupture history, and subtype or genetic syndrome evaluation where relevant, with the allocation pathway recorded as non-standard review with no automatic entitlement. Owner: transplant oncology intake coordinator.

Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead. Unlike a malignancy board this one must keep slots for surveillance cases: the decision not to operate on a 5.5 cm lesion is a board decision and should not be made in a corridor. Owner: coordinator.
Urgent lane — a same-day route for acute haemorrhage and a same-week slot for the pregnant patient with a growing lesion, both with chair approval. Owner: chair.

Attendance — hepatology, hepatobiliary surgery, transplant surgery, diagnostic radiology with a named liver MRI reader, interventional radiology, liver pathology, and coordination are required. Metabolic genetics attends every glycogen storage disease case; vascular expertise every congenital portosystemic shunt case; obstetrics every pregnancy case; bariatric medicine every case where weight is the driver and a major resection is contemplated. Owners: specialty leads.

Imaging — the named liver MRI reader reviews the study with all priors side by side, states which subtype criteria were applied and which were not assessable, and reports diameter on a fixed convention, because the growth trigger is a 20% change. Owner: diagnostic radiology.

Pathology — expert liver pathology review is mandatory for every male adenoma, every borderline or atypical lesion, and every lesion reported from outside. The four-antibody panel is standard; CTNNB1 sequencing with exon and codon is requested wherever activation is suspected or a transplant route may be invoked. Owner: pathology.

Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, and one documented alternative considered. For a surveillance decision the output must state the next interval, the modality, the growth threshold that will trigger reassessment, and the date the plan itself expires. Owner: chair.

Risk-factor ownership — the oestrogen or androgen withdrawal and the weight plan each get a named owner at the same meeting, with a review date. An unassigned weight plan is the commonest reason the 6-month scan shows nothing has changed. Owner: named owner.
Documentation — an Epic note within one business day in the agreed structured format, including what the patient was told about the alternative not chosen. Owner: named owner.

Registry — every case closed in the registry with the decision, the modality delivered, the specimen or explant subtype, and the concordance between the preoperative and the final diagnosis. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is told the recommendation, the interval and who owns the next step; patients under surveillance are returned to their referrer with a written plan rather than retained. Community-referring relationships are protected explicitly. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Proportion of adenoma referrals characterised on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent before the first board discussion, and the proportion whose diagnosis changed after that scan (approval item 1).
Subtype assignment rate, the method used (imaging, immunohistochemistry, sequencing), and concordance between the preoperative subtype and the resection specimen (approval item 2).
Expert liver pathology review rate in male adenomas and borderline lesions, and the rate at which the diagnosis changed on review (approval item 4).
Time from diagnosis to documented cessation of oestrogen or androgen exposure, and to a named owner for the weight plan (approval item 3).

Diameter trajectory of every adenoma over 5 cm under surveillance, reported as time to fall below 5 cm or time to intervention, against the published benchmarks of 8.5-15.3% regressed at 26 weeks, 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks and 58.5% at a median 104 weeks — the test of whether the local decision point is set at the right time (approval items 3 and 16).
Intervention mix — resection, embolisation, ablation, surveillance — with diameter change, Clavien-Dindo complication grade, and any subsequent intervention (approval item 5).

Malignant transformation and occult carcinoma rate in resection specimens and explants, by sex, size, background liver and preoperative subtype, reported per patient and per lesion — the single most important number this disease generates locally, and the only way to find out whether it is the centimetres or the driver mutation that matters here (approval items 7, 14, 15 and 17).
Haemorrhage events: lesion size, exophytic status, segment, pregnancy status, management route, and whether residual viable lesion was resected afterwards (approval item 6).
Pregnancy outcomes: diameter, subtype, growth during pregnancy, intervention, mode of delivery, and any haemorrhage through the puerperium (approval item 9).

Adenoma transplant pathway, if opened: route named, review-board decision, waitlist events, donor source, explant concordance, graft and patient survival, and malignant transformation (approval item 10).

Surveillance adherence: the proportion of planned interval scans performed within 30 days of their due date, and the proportion of patients lost to follow-up — in a young, well population this is the failure mode that actually occurs.

Resections performed on lesions under 50 mm, as a proportion of all adenoma resections, with the final diagnosis of each — the national benchmark is 20% of resections below 50 mm, of which 70% had their diagnosis changed and 21% proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia (approval items 1, 13 and 17).

Concordance between the preoperative working diagnosis and subtype and the final pathology, reported annually with denominators and separately for male patients and for lesions under 50 mm (approval item 17).

For embolisation: diameter change, Society of Interventional Radiology complication grade, symptom status at 3 months, and the proportion who subsequently required resection — the published benchmarks are 10% grade D complications, one death in 59 patients, unchanged symptoms (P=0.134) and 34% proceeding to surgery (approval item 5).

approvals.q: Is MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent mandatory before any adenoma is managed as an adenoma, and who may waive it?
approvals.why: 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI in the prospective cohort — a lesion needing no follow-up at all. This is an access and cost question as much as a clinical one, so it needs a written answer rather than a preference.
approvals.audit: Audit: proportion characterised before first board discussion, and proportion whose diagnosis changed.

approvals.q: Does the programme adopt routine subtyping — a standing four-antibody panel on every specimen and biopsy, with CTNNB1 exon and codon sequencing where activation is suspected, and prostaglandin D synthase for the sonic hedgehog subgroup?
approvals.why: EASL 2016 states there is no justification for recommending routine subtyping. The molecular data since, and the local transplant protocol's own molecular route, both assume it is available. Those two positions cannot both be acted on. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Registry: subtype assigned, method, concordance with the resection specimen.

approvals.q: How long may risk-factor modification run before a persistent lesion over 5 cm is treated — EASL's 6 months, or 12, or longer in a lesion that is still falling?
approvals.why: EASL and ACG indicate resection at 6 months. At that point only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have fallen below 5 cm, against 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks and 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks, with no complication during the whole of that follow-up and time to regression strongly size-dependent (median 63 weeks under 7 cm, 208 weeks over 10 cm). The six-month trigger therefore captures roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually cross the line. The cohort's authors proposed 12 months for typical non-beta-catenin adenomas in women; 79% of responding European experts already decline the rule; and the only GRADE-appraised guideline grades the 6-month decision point very low quality, conditional. Decide the number, and decide whether it differs by baseline diameter.
approvals.audit: Audit: time to fall below 5 cm or to intervention, for every adenoma over 5 cm under surveillance.

approvals.q: Does the programme resect every male adenoma irrespective of size, and is expert liver pathology review with sequencing mandatory in every male case?
approvals.why: EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all say resect, the last of them at very low quality of evidence, conditional. The male evidence is a 47% versus 4% transformation prevalence in one tertiary surgical series whose transformed lesions had a median diameter of 10 cm, an approximately ten-fold male excess in a second, and male sex as an independent predictor at an odds ratio of 18.9 (8.5-44.2). Against that, the diagnostic label is unreliable in exactly this group: 50% of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert review with 4 beta-catenin mutations found only by sequencing, and 78% of male resections in a national audit had their diagnosis changed. The full-text read also withdrew the 23.8% occult-carcinoma figure this page previously used — the supported figure is 4 transformations in 27 male adenomas — and found no cohort supporting observation of any male adenoma. So the question is whether the rule is retained because men are at higher risk or because the diagnosis cannot be trusted in men; the answer changes what the pathology requirement is for.
approvals.audit: Registry: sex, size, subtype, sequencing result, decision, specimen finding.

approvals.q: Is elective transarterial embolisation accepted as a first-line alternative to resection in a good surgical candidate who prefers it?
approvals.why: EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The data since show 84% surgery avoidance after elective embolisation, on 49 patients from multiple small series, and a fall in median diameter from 76 to 48 mm. Against that: 10% grade D complications, one reported death three months after the procedure, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, no symptom improvement at 3 months (P=0.134), viable tissue and no histology left behind in a disease where 20-40% of presumed adenomas prove to be something else, and a pooled follow-up of 31 months too short to detect transformation. That is a shared decision the programme should endorse or decline explicitly, with the harms disclosed, rather than leave to individual preference.
approvals.audit: Registry: modality, diameter change, complication grade, subsequent intervention.

approvals.q: What is the acute haemorrhage pathway, and who owns it out of hours?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question. EASL's recommendation to embolise the unstable patient is evidence level III, and the practical failure mode is a young woman arriving at a hospital that cannot embolise, with no named transfer route. The interval to the post-embolisation re-imaging that decides whether she needs a resection is also undefined by any study.
approvals.audit: Audit: haemorrhage events with size, position, management route, time to definitive control, and whether residual viable lesion was resected.

approvals.q: Does the programme adopt a composite operative trigger — 5 cm, or 20% growth, or exophytic position, or visible lesional arteries, or a segment II-III location — in place of diameter alone, and who will verify the figures behind it?
approvals.why: This item cannot be decided yet, and that is now the honest answer. The positional and vascular effect sizes this page previously quoted in support could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn; what the supporting paper does establish is a fitted cut-point at 35 mm with bleeding in 5.4% below against 53% above, in a retrospective cohort whose own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected, with grades I to III pooled, no beta-catenin adenoma identified in 195 lesions and 48% unclassifiable. Adopting a composite trigger would mean operating on some lesions below 5 cm, which no guideline endorses. Before deciding, someone should read that paper's positional analysis directly and report the numbers.
approvals.audit: Registry: for every haemorrhage, which trigger features were present and whether they had been recorded prospectively.

approvals.q: Does the transplant protocol's S45 and exon 7/8 restriction stand as written?
approvals.why: The protocol places S45 exon 3 with the exon 7/8 alterations as not qualifying the molecular route alone. The genotype-phenotype data make S45 a special case rather than a low-risk one — a weak activator in benign tumours, found at similar frequency in mutated adenomas and carcinomas, and duplicated to high activity in most carcinomas. The restriction is defensible as organ stewardship but not as a statement about risk, and the NLRB narrative should say which of the two it is.
approvals.audit: Registry: CTNNB1 exon and codon for every sequenced adenoma, the route decision taken on it, and the explant or specimen finding.

approvals.q: What is the programme's position on a 5 to 7 cm adenoma in a woman who wants to conceive now, and who counsels her?
approvals.why: EASL recommends treating a large lesion before pregnancy; the prospective data stop at 5 cm; every reported pregnancy-associated haemorrhage occurred at 6.5 cm or above, and a fatal one is reported. A European survey identified this as one of the two areas of greatest practice variation. The counselling needs hepatology, hepatobiliary surgery, interventional radiology and obstetrics in the room together.
approvals.audit: Registry: diameter, subtype, intervention or none, growth during pregnancy, mode of delivery, haemorrhage, maternal and fetal outcome.

approvals.q: Does the programme open an adenoma transplant route at all, and under whose governance?
approvals.why: Hepatocellular adenoma is not a standardised exception. The whole indication rests on 142 US transplants over 33 years with 18.3% mortality over a median 62.9 months and 9.0% waitlist mortality in patients of median age 34.5 and median MELD 8 — so almost all of that mortality is treatment-attributable — plus 49 European adenomatosis transplants with three operative deaths, five retransplantations, three fatal recurrences and true transformation in only 17 of 49 explants. The US registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas; the European one miscoded a quarter of its cases; neither has a comparison group managed without transplantation; and 61.3% of US recipients received exception points while about a tenth met the stated criteria. Graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and it should be made with those numbers in front of the committee.
approvals.audit: Registry required if opened: route named, lesion dataset, review-board decision, waitlist events, donor source, explant concordance, graft and patient survival.

approvals.q: Who verifies the live OPTN Policy 9.4 and 9.5 text and the current transplant-oncology guidance before each submission, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: The local protocol marks the standardised-versus-non-standard classification, the Class 5 imaging criteria and submission routes, and the extension cycle and governing subsection as VERIFY, and requires a recheck immediately before committee adoption, submission or extension. None of those has been verified for this page.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus policy version and date, with an agreed recheck cycle and a record of the check against each submission.

approvals.q: Who owns the next revision of this page, and what triggers it?
approvals.why: EASL 2016 is the last full guideline and a decade of subtype, male-adenoma, diagnostic-accuracy and surveillance data has accumulated behind it — including, since 2021, a direct test of the threshold hypothesis that returned a negative, a demonstration that the six-month decision point is mistimed, contemporary surveillance rates one to two orders of magnitude below the historical figures, and a WHO classification that recommends resecting one subtype irrespective of size. ACG 2024 restates the 2016 rules without engaging any of it. A Delphi or consensus update has been formally proposed in the literature. The page should name an owner and a trigger now rather than silently age.
approvals.audit: Named owner, review date, and a standing check for a new EASL or AASLD benign liver tumour guideline.

approvals.q: How is the 5 cm number described to a patient, and in the operative consent — as a threshold, or as a convention?
approvals.why: Not a clinical question but a consent question, and the full-text read makes it unavoidable. EASL calls 5 cm the accepted clinically relevant size cut off and grades the recommendation II-3 with conditional strength; the only GRADE-appraised guideline grades every size-based recommendation very low quality, conditional; the study that tested the threshold hypothesis most directly found size acting continuously at an odds ratio of 1.02 per millimetre and stated that no threshold size was identified; and 79% of responding European experts decline the rule. A patient told that her 5.5 cm adenoma has crossed a risk threshold has been told something the evidence does not support. Agree a form of words, put it in the consent template, and put it in the radiology report footer.
approvals.audit: Audit: a sample of consent forms and clinic letters for adenoma resections, checked for whether the described basis for the operation matches the agreed wording.

approvals.q: When size and subtype conflict — a 4 cm beta-catenin exon 3 lesion, or a 7 cm HNF1A-inactivated one that is shrinking — which takes precedence, and who decides?
approvals.why: This is the commonest real decision and no document answers it. The Italian guideline recommends biopsy specifically to identify exon 3 and sonic hedgehog adenomas (its PICO 9) and simultaneously keeps 5 cm as the resection trigger (its PICO 11), without specifying which governs when they disagree. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that exon 3 adenomas are resected whatever their size, but cites no cohort. EASL's rule is explicitly size-first and subtype-blind above the threshold. The molecular data support subtype in both directions — 2 of 14 women with an at-risk profile under 5 cm transformed against 1 of 101 without — but on two events. Write the precedence rule down, with the proviso that it will be applied to a subtype assignment that is often made without sequencing.
approvals.audit: Registry: for every case where size and subtype pointed different ways, the decision taken, who took it, and the specimen or follow-up outcome.

approvals.q: Does the registry record outcomes per patient as well as per lesion, with the denominator stated?
approvals.why: The single biggest statistical problem in the literature supporting the 5 cm rule is per-lesion versus per-patient conflation: the pooled systematic review reports haemorrhage in 27.2% of patients but 15.8% of lesions, a near-twofold difference, and the series with the strongest-looking size gradient counted 365 adenomas in 122 patients, which drives the small-lesion rates down arithmetically. A programme that does not fix its own denominator convention will reproduce the same artefact in its own audit and will not be able to compare its numbers with anyone else's.
approvals.audit: Registry specification: every rate reported with its numerator, denominator and whether it is per patient or per lesion.

approvals.q: Does the programme accept extended observation of a lesion over 5 cm as a board-sanctioned option rather than a deviation, and what stops it?
approvals.why: Four fifths of responding European experts already decline routine resection above 5 cm, the contemporary surveillance figures are 88.5% stable or regressed with 0.5% symptomatic bleeding and 0.8% transformation, a surveillance-dominant 164-patient cohort reports 1.8% rupture and no transformation among those watched, and 58.5% of lesions over 5 cm fall below it eventually with no complications recorded during observation. Against that, every one of those datasets describes lesions already selected as safe to watch, and in five of seven pooled studies lesions were removed from surveillance as soon as they grew. If extended observation is to be offered it needs named stopping rules — growth, a change of subtype information, pregnancy intention, symptoms, loss to follow-up — and a date at which the plan itself expires.
approvals.audit: Registry: every lesion over 5 cm under observation, with the stopping rules recorded at the outset and the reason recorded whenever one fires.

approvals.q: Does the programme audit its own concordance between preoperative and final diagnosis, and publish it internally?
approvals.why: The full-text read makes this the most informative number the programme can generate. Nationally, 43% of resections for presumed adenoma had a different postoperative diagnosis, rising to 70% below 50 mm and 78% in men, with focal nodular hyperplasia in 21% of resected sub-50 mm lesions; 50% of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert review; and 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions in a prospective cohort were focal nodular hyperplasia. A local concordance rate is the only way to know whether this programme's preoperative assessment is better or worse than that, and it is the field that makes every other registry field interpretable.
approvals.audit: Registry: preoperative working diagnosis and subtype against final pathology for every resection and explant, reported annually with denominators.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the depot. All 46 papers behind this page were read in full and abstracted, each with the authors' stated limitations and an independent critique recorded, and every evidence string on the page was checked against that abstraction. Fifty-eight evidence strings changed, across 119 fields. Six are corrections large enough to change what the page tells a surgeon, and they are set out in the honest section: that 5 cm is a convention rather than a derived threshold, which the page now states in the size gate itself and grades D; that the six-month decision point is mistimed, because only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have regressed below 5 cm at 26 weeks against 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks with no complication during that follow-up; that the apparent size gradient in the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French series is largely a per-lesion artefact of a resect-everything policy whose sub-2 cm stratum is incidental microadenomas found inside specimens removed for a larger lesion; that transarterial embolisation caused one reported death and left 34% of patients still requiring surgery, where the earlier draft stated that no deaths were reported; that the 23.8% occult-carcinoma figure the earlier draft attributed to a US male resection series is not supported and has been withdrawn, the supported figure being 4 transformations in 27 male adenomas; and that the positional and vascular bleeding effect sizes the earlier draft attributed to a prospective imaging cohort could not be confirmed and have been withdrawn, with the composite-trigger proposal and approval item 7 left explicitly undecided until someone reads that paper's positional analysis. Grades were revised where the critique warranted it rather than from study design alone: the 5 cm resection trigger, the 6-month reimaging interval, the composite positional trigger and thermal ablation were all downgraded, and the pregnancy recommendation for lesions under 5 cm moved from B to C because zero ruptures in 51 pregnancies has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7% and both pregnancy cohorts were pre-filtered by the rule they are used to relax. Six papers newly obtained for this revision have been added: the French multicentre bleeding cohort that modelled size continuously and found no threshold (Ann Surg 2021, PMID 34334644); the Dutch nationwide audit of diagnostic accuracy in resections for presumed adenoma (Hepatol Commun 2022, PMID 36324268); the Korean nationwide clinical, radiological and pathological series (Liver Int 2024, PMID 39526315); the contemporary surveillance-dominant natural-history cohort (Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2026, PMID 42214026); the narrative review presenting the hepatocellular adenoma and carcinoma classification of the WHO 6th edition (Virchows Arch 2026, PMID 42678415), which is cited throughout as a review of that classification and not as the classification itself, which has not been read for this page; and the imaging-surveillance meta-analysis already present from the first draft and now read in full (Abdom Radiol 2026, PMID 41364225). Two papers named in the gap scan were not obtained and are not cited anywhere: McDermott 2021 (PMID 34687281) and Elfrink 2021 (PMID 33478819). Volume and page numbers were not available for the five newly added references and have not been invented; each is cited by journal, year, title and PMID, with that limitation stated in the reference entry. Two references remain cited from abstract only, because they are not in the full-text depot: the review of ruptured hepatocellular adenoma management (Dig Surg 2010, PMID 20357452), which supports the acute-haemorrhage sequence in gate 5, and the French-language review of hepatic lesions in altered liver vascularisation (Rev Med Liege 2025, PMID 39950525), which supports the vascular-liver-disease string in gate 8. Both of those gates should be read as the weakest-sourced on the page. Where the earlier draft carried a figure that the full-text abstraction does not contain and that figure bore argumentative weight, it has been replaced with a depot-supported figure or removed and the removal disclosed; purely descriptive detail from the abstract-only draft has in a few places been left in place, and anyone re-reading this page against the sources should expect to find such detail rather than assume it was verified. The page was originally built from EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours (J Hepatol 2016;65:386-398), which remains the last full guideline for this disease; the ACG Clinical Guideline on Focal Liver Lesions (Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:1235-1271); the Italian multisociety benign liver lesions guideline of 2022, which the full-text read shows to be the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework and which grades every size-based adenoma recommendation very low quality of evidence (D), conditional; the French multisociety guidance of 2021, whose every adenoma recommendation is graded C1, C2 or D2; the Nault molecular classification of hepatocellular adenoma (Gastroenterology 2017;152:880-894.e6) and the Rebouissou CTNNB1 genotype-phenotype study (Hepatology 2016;64:2047-2061) for subtype and mutation risk; and the primary literature since 2016 on subtype-specific risk, male adenomas, surveillance outcomes, embolisation, thermal ablation, pregnancy, adenomatosis and transplantation, all of it listed in the reference library with PMIDs verified individually against PubMed on 6 October 2026. The transplant gate and quick reference 4 come from the local UTHealth Houston Hepatic Adenoma Liver Transplant Protocol V3, policy review date 21 September 2026, which is the authority for that gate and for nothing else on the page; the board and front-door operating content draws on the UTHealth Houston / Memorial Hermann Master Workup and Staging CPG and its hepatic adenoma staging row. Allocation statements are reproduced from that protocol and have not been independently checked against the live OPTN Policy 9.4 and 9.5 postings or the December 2025 transplant-oncology review-board guidance; the protocol marks several of them VERIFY and they remain unverified here. The 2025 UK NHSBT Liver Advisory Group guidance has now been read: it assigns patients with benign liver tumours to four eligibility categories by consensus with no underlying cohort, and because it does not state how adenoma size, number, subtype or prior intervention map onto those categories, its criteria are still not paraphrased on this page. One earlier source gap is recorded for completeness: the file supplied as the European adenomatosis source contained an unrelated French conference paper with no adenoma content, so the adenomatosis evidence here comes instead from the Tours long-term observational cohort (J Hepatol 2019;71:1184-1192), the European Liver Transplant Registry adenomatosis series (Liver Transpl 2016;22:516-526) and EASL's own multiple-lesion section. This page remains a draft. Unlike the five existing disease pages it transcribes no ratified system roadmap, because none exists for hepatocellular adenoma: outside the transplant gate, every position on it is a proposal assembled from published guidelines and primary literature and awaiting multidisciplinary and institutional ratification. The full-text read has made the page more honest about the strength of its own recommendations; it has not made any of them policy. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
